### FOREWORD

This series of articles on Zuñi Bread-stuff was first published in *The Millstone* of Indianapolis (a trade magazine that has long since stopped publication), in its issues spanning from volume IX, January 1884, to volume X, August 1885. Later, an attempt was made to reprint the articles in a shortened form in *Milling* of Chicago, but only the first nine chapters appeared this way, spanning from volume III, no. 2, July 1893, to volume IV, no. 4, March 1894, when their publication ended. Mr. Cushing’s account of the subject is so filled with information regarding not only the food products of the Zuñi tribe—with whom he lived as an adopted member from 1879 until 1884—but also their methods of preparation and the myths, ceremonies, and daily customs related to them.

---

<meta>This page continues the Foreword, explaining the rationale for the republication of Cushing's work and the editorial standards applied to the new edition.</meta>

### ZUÑI BREADSTUFF

It is unnecessary to say that Frank Hamilton Cushing was in such close contact with the Zuñi that he was thoroughly familiar with the topics he wrote about concerning those interesting people. It is for the purpose of making them accessible to students of American ethnology, and especially of the Pueblo Indians, that the articles referred to—which until now were practically inaccessible—are republished in this series.

In preparing the work for publication, no attempt has been made to change the original text, except where it obviously required improvement in punctuation, the correction of typographical and spelling errors, consistency in the spelling of native terms, and the conversion of various terms and expressions to roman type from italics where they were not needed for direct emphasis. All the illustrations used in the original articles are reproduced here, somewhat smaller in size, and several photographic plates from negatives by Mr. Jesse L. Nusbaum, further illustrating the subject, have been introduced.

# FOREWORD
VIII
AND MONOGRAPHS

The late Major John Wesley Powell, founder and first director of the Bureau of American Ethnology, was quoted from the Twenty-first Annual Report of that institution:

> "Frank Hamilton Cushing was born in Northeast, Pennsylvania, July 22, 1857. Initially physically frail, he withdrew from the usual social circles of childhood and youth and developed a remarkable connection with nature; as his frail body’s growth slowed, his mental powers grew in such a way that they separated him even further from more conventional peers. In childhood, he found 'sermons in stones and books in running brooks'; and in youth, his school was the forest around his father’s homestead in central New York. There, his passion for nature intensified, and the habit of interpreting things according to natural principles, rather than conventional rules, grew so strong that it directed his later life. Meanwhile, freed from the constant drain on his mind caused by the friction of social relationships, his mind gained strength and power; he became a genius."

<summary>This page presents a biographical excerpt by Major John Wesley Powell describing Frank Hamilton Cushing’s early life, physical frailty, and his unconventional education in nature. It highlights how Cushing's isolation from social norms allowed his intellect to develop into what Powell describes as genius.</summary>

> “At nine years of age, Cushing’s attention was caught by Indian arrowheads found in his neighborhood. He began a collection that grew into a museum and laboratory, which he housed in a wigwam he built in a secluded part of the family homestead. His interest and knowledge grew until, at eighteen, he went to Cornell University already an expert capable of instructing the teachers. Perhaps because of his close connection with nature, he early on fell into a habit of thought not unlike that of the primitive arrow maker; even before he knew living Indians, he grew to sympathize with Indian art, Indian methods, and Indian motives. So, in his wigwam laboratory and later at Cornell and elsewhere, he began to reproduce chipped stone arrowheads and other aboriginal artifacts using processes similar to those of native artisans. In this art, he attained a unique degree of skill, and through it, he gained a unique understanding of the methods of primitive people. In 1874, at the age of seventeen, he sent to Secretary Baird <note>Spencer Fullerton Baird, the second Secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.</note> an account of the Antiquities of Orleans County, New York,

One of the results was the organization of the <term>Hemenway Archeological Expedition</term>, endowed by the late Mrs. Mary Hemenway of Boston; in 1886–88, Mr. Cushing had charge of the work. Subsequently, he returned to the service of the Bureau and began preparing the records of his research in Zuñi for publication; a part of this material was published in the Thirteenth Report under the title ‘Outlines of Zuñi Creation Myths.’”

# FOREWORD
13
AND MONOGRAPHS
VIII

His health failing to an extent requiring a change, he was assigned to duty in Florida, where he made an archaeological survey no less remarkable for the breadth of view with which it was conducted than for the wealth of material produced from shell mounds and peat-lined lagoons. He was actively engaged in preparing the results of this work for publication when a slight accident (the swallowing of a fish bone) proved too much for the vital thread of his life, which was never strong and was much enfeebled by wholehearted and absorbing devotion to duty under trying conditions in Zuñi and in Florida. So his professional career ended. He died April 10, 1900.

> “Cushing was a man of genius. The history of the human world has been shaped by a few men; the multitudes have lived and worked and ended their days under the leadership of these few. Most of the geniuses who have shaped the history of later times shone as intellectual luminaries alone. Cushing stood out not only as a man of intellect, but preeminently as a master of those manual concepts to which

have attained perfect union. Cushing belonged to this class of men; yet the application of his genius was peculiar, even unique, in that his efforts were spent in interpreting the inventions of others rather than in making inventions of his own. This application of his powers made him successful beyond parallel in retracing the paths followed by early humans in their slow advance toward manual and mechanical skill; and it was through this peculiar application that Cushing’s richest contributions to the science of man were made.

> “By reason of his peculiar insight into primitive devices and motives, Cushing was a teacher to his coworkers, even to those who were older than he was. His mind responded readily to the impact of new sights, new thoughts, and new knowledge; therefore, he was fertile in hypothesis, fruitful in suggestion, an **avant-courier** in research, and a leader in interpretation. All his associates profited by his originality and learned much from him. The debt of American ethnology to Cushing is large.”

# ZUÑI BREADSTUFF

## BY FRANK HAMILTON CUSHING

### CHAPTER I

#### CREATION, AND THE ORIGIN OF CORN <note>1</note>

WATCHING one day a white-haired Zuñi grandmother who was stirring some yellow batter vigorously with a bundle of splints, I asked her what she was making. "Hoe-cakes," she answered, although she called them *mu'-we*.

"How do you make them?" I inquired.

"*Sa-k'o, o'-lut-si-na ta k'ia'-kok-shi, hi-ni-na hâ i'-ya si'; tem kwi'l-ip-nan, hâ ko-la ma-we ta i'-sha-nan wo-lu, shél-an-an ul-üp, he'-po-k'on wo'-tap, te'-na-lap, u-li'-hap,—tchim i'-to-na-k'ia, a'ya-naie!*'"—replied the old woman.

# ZUÑI BREADSTUFF
VIII
->INDIAN NOTES<-

This is as difficult as Zuñi milling; but I will try to grind it into English.

> “Meal, soft corn-flour, and good water, I mix equally; then, while stirring, I put in red pepper, salt, and suet. I roll this into husks, place them all into an oven, and shut the hole; when time has passed, I take them out. Now then, they are ready for eating!”

Do not imagine the old woman knew no other way of making corn food. The ancient Zuñis are just as resourceful with their corn as the Chinese are with their rice.

Indeed, corn is so important to the Zuñi that it plays an essential part not only in his daily life but also in his industrial, religious, and mythological life, and even in the tales with which he amuses children by the fireside in winter.

So that this may be better understood by those governed by a culture totally different from that of the Zuñis; and so that the many observances, ceremonies, and formulas connected with corn—its growth, treatment, and preparation for food, to be described hereafter—may not seem insignificant—

meaningless, it is necessary that an outline of the Zuñi mythology connected with corn, and at least some of the philosophy and folklore which have grown out of this mythology, be recorded.

Thus, by following me in the pursuit of a useful purpose, I anticipate that my readers will find some of the interest and pleasure I experienced when, on long winter nights, I listened, in the light of piñon fires on Zuñi hearthstones, to the recitations which first gave me knowledge of these strange beliefs and things.

While listening in this way, I once heard a Zuñi priest say:

> “Five things alone are necessary for the sustenance and comfort of the ‘dark ones’ <note>Indians</note> among the children of earth:
> “The sun, who is the Father of all.
> “The earth, who is the Mother of men.
> “The water, who is the Grandfather.
> “The fire, who is the Grandmother.
> “Our brothers and sisters the Corn, and the seeds of growing things.”

<sig>VIII</sig>

> "Who among men and the creatures could live without the Sun Father? For his light brings day, warms and gladdens the Earth Mother with rain which flows forth in the water we drink and causes the flesh of the Earth Mother to yield seeds abundantly; while these—are they not cooked by the brand of fire which warms us in winter?"

That he reasoned well may be better understood if we follow for a while the teachings that instructed his logic. These relate that:

First, there was sublime darkness, which did not vanish until the "Ancient Father of the Sun" came, revealing universal waters. These were, except for him, all that existed.

The Sun Father thought to change the face of the waters and cause life to replace their desolation.

He rubbed the surface of his flesh, thus drawing forth *yep'na* <note>This term refers to a vital substance or essence of life</note>.²

He rolled the *yep'na* into two balls. From his high and "ancient place among the spaces" (*Te'-thlä-shi-na-kwin*) he cast

forth one of these balls and it fell upon the surface of the waters. There, like a drop of deer fat on hot broth, this ball melted and spread far and wide like a film over the great waters, constantly growing until it sank into them.

Then the Sun Father cast forth the other ball, and it fell, spreading out and growing even larger than the first had. It displaced so much of the waters that it rested upon the first ball. In time, the first became a great being—our Mother, the Earth; and the second became another great being—our Father, the Sky. Thus the universal fluid was divided into the “embracing waters of the World” below, and the “embracing waters of the Sky” above. Behold! This is why the Sky Father is as blue as the ocean which is the home of the Earth Mother; even his flesh is blue, as the far-away mountains appear, though they are the flesh of the Earth Mother.

Now, while the Sky Father and the Earth Mother were together, the Earth Mother conceived in her ample wombs—which were the four great underworlds or caves—

"How shall it be?" said the one to the other. "How, when they are born, shall our children survive, and who shall guide them?"

"Behold!" said the Sky Father. He spread his hand high and wide with the hollow palm downward. He stuck yellow grains like corn into all the lines and wrinkles of his palm and fingers. "Thus," said he, "I shall, as it were, hold my hand forever above you and your children, and the yellow grains shall represent many shining points which shall guide and light these, our children, when the Sun Father is not near."

Gaze at the sky at nighttime! Is it not the palm of the Great Father, and are the stars not still to be seen in the many lines of his hand?

"Ah, yes!" said the Earth Mother, "yet my tiny children may not wander over my lap and bosom without guidance, even in the light of the Sun Father; therefore, behold!"

She took a great terraced bowl and poured water into it; she spat upon the water, and, whipping it rapidly with her fingers, it was soon beaten into foam as the soap-weed froths, and the foam rose high up around the rim of the bowl. The Earth Mother blew on the foam. Flake after flake broke off, and bursting, cast spray downward into the bowl.

“See,” she said, “this bowl is, as it were, the world, the rim its farthest limits, and the foam-edged terraces all around are my features, which they shall call mountains. By these they shall name countries and be guided from place to place, and from them white clouds shall rise, float away, and, bursting, shed spray, so that my children may drink of the water of life, and from my substance add to the flesh of their being. You have said you will watch over them when the Sun Father is absent, but you are the cold being; I am the warm one. Therefore, at night, when you watch, my children shall nestle in my bosom and find there warmth, strength, and length of life from one daylight to another.”

Is not the bowl the emblem of the Earth, our mother? For from it we draw both food and drink, as a baby draws nourishment from its mother’s breast; and just as the rim of a bowl is round, so too is the horizon, terraced with mountains from which the clouds rise. Is not woman the warm being, and man the cold? For while woman sits shivering as she cooks by the fire in the house-room, man goes forth, paying little heed to the storms of winter, to hunt the deer and gather bundles of pine wood.

Yet, alas! Men and the creatures remained bound in the lowest womb of the Earth Mother, for she and the Sky Father feared to deliver them, just as a mother fears for the fate of her first offspring.

Then the Ancient Sun pitied the children of Earth. So that they might quickly see his light, he cast a glance upon a foam-cap floating out upon the great waters. Immediately, the foam-cap was imbued with life and bore twin children, brothers to one another—older and younger, for one was born before the other. Alas! It was as dark as the world had been before the arrival of the Sun, and the brothers found the men and other beings sadly lamenting their fate. Thus it happened that they and their brothers, sisters, and children, even to the present day, were named after the things they chose in the days when everything was new. In this way our nation was divided into many clans (<term>*a'-no-ti-we*</term>) of brothers and sisters who may not marry one another, but must marry from one clan into another. To some of the elders of these bands and clans was given something that was to be, above all other things, precious. For instance, the Bear and Crane clans were given the <term>*mu'-et-ton-ne*</term>, or medicine seed of hail and snow. For does the bear not go into his den, and does the crane not appear when the storms of hail and snow arrive?

To all of these peoples it was told that they should wander for many generations toward the land where the Sun brings the daylight (eastward), until at last they would reach the "middle of the world." There, their children should dwell forever over the heart of our Earth Mother until their days are numbered and the light of Zuñi grows dark.

The "twin brothers of light" guided them toward this unknown country. In those times, a day meant a year, and a night another, so that four days and nights meant eight years. For many days the people wandered eastward, slaying game for their meat, gathering seeds from grasses and weeds for their bread, and binding rushes about their loins for their clothing; they did not know until afterward the flesh of the cotton- and yucca-mothers.

Many of the great monsters and predatory beings were changed in an instant into enduring rock or shriveled into twisted idols which the hunter and priest-warrior know best how to value. Behold! Their forms along every mountainside and ravine, and in the far western valleys and plains, still endure—as do the tracks of the ancestors of men and beings, the children of earth. Yet some of the predatory beings were spared, so that the world might not become overpopulated and followed by starvation, and so that men might breathe in their spirits and be inspired with the hearts of warriors and hunters.

The works of the ancients were marvelous, both in good and evil. Alas! along with the others, there came those filled with the seed of sorcery. Their evil works caused discord among men, and through fear and anger, men were divided from one another. Other men had been born before our ancients, and our fathers sometimes overtook these people and did not look upon them peacefully but challenged them—even though, were they not their elder brothers?

Thus it happened when our ancients came to their fourth resting place on their eastward journey, which they named *Shi-po-lo-lon-K'ai-a*, or "Place of Misty Waters," that a clan of people called the *A'-tâ-a*, or Seed people, already lived there. “Brothers indeed we are, each one to the other,” said the people to the strangers, “and may we not journey together seeking the middle of the world?”

“Yes, we may,” replied the strangers, “and of the flesh of our maidens you may eat, no longer seeking the seeds of the grasses, and of your water we may drink, no longer wondering where we shall find it; thus shall each help the other to life and contentment. You shall pray and cut prayer-plumes; we shall sing, and our maidens shall dance so that all may be delighted and that it may be for the best. But beware! no mortal must approach the persons of our maidens.”

From then on, many of the *A’-tâ-a* and the Seed clan journeyed together, until at last the Sun, Macaw, and some other clanspeople found the middle of the world; while others still wandered in search of it, not to join their brothers for many generations, over the heart of the Earth

Day after day, season after season, year after year, the people of the Seed clan and the <term>*A'-tâ-a*</term>—who were named together as the Corn clan, or people—prepared, and their maidens danced the dance of the <term>*Thla-he-kwe*</term> <note>7</note>, or "Beautiful Corn Wands," until their children grew weary and yearned for other amusements.

Sometimes the people saw thick mists floating and hanging low over Thunder Mountain. <note>8</note> At such times, near the Cave of the Rainbow, a beautiful halo would spring forth, in the midst of which the many-colored garments of the rainbow himself could be seen, and soft, sweet music—stranger than the whistling winds in a mountain of pines—floated fitfully down the valley. At last, the priests and elders gathered in council and determined to send their two chief warriors (<term>Priests of the Bow</term>) to the Cavern of the Rainbow, so that it might be determined what strange people made those sights and sounds. # ZUÑI BREADSTUFF
## VIII

> "Just as a mother gives life to her offspring from her own blood and being, so have these maidens given you their own flesh. Once more they give their flesh to you, as if it were their children. From the beginning of the new sun each year, you shall treasure their gift; during the moon of the sacred fire, during the moon of the snow-broken boughs, during the moon of the great sand-driving winds, and during the moon of the lesser sand-driving winds, you shall treasure their flesh. Then, in the new soil which the winter winds and waters have brought, you shall bury their flesh as you bury the flesh of the dead. Just as the flesh of the dead decays, so shall their flesh decay; and as another being (the soul) springs from the flesh of the dead, so from their flesh shall spring a new being, similar to the first, yet in eight-fold abundance. You shall eat of this and be free from hunger. Look at these maidens; they are beautiful and perfect. Since this flesh of theirs is derived from them, it shall grant beauty and physical perfection to those whom it feeds, just like the maidens from whom it came."

## CHAPTER II

### THE ORIGIN OF THE DRAGONFLY AND OF THE CORN PRIESTS, OR GUARDIANS OF THE SEED

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' in a square frame with ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
THERE is nothing about Indian life so interesting as its lore. The Indian, like his possible Mongolian ancestor, lives less in the present than in the past. His spirit loves to roam through the dark, wild vistas of antiquity and dream of the marvels which he devoutly believes caused all things to become as they are. To him, the youth of the world, with its beautiful visions of what is to be, has fled; and however young he may be, he is like a man in his dotage <note>senile old age</note>. There is a reason for all this, aside from his nationality. To no man on earth does the future seem so gloomy and fateful as it does to the Indian; the past stands in such heroic, glorious contrast with it. Therefore, like a poor beast, driven by the storm-blast to

<summary>This chapter introduces the importance of lore in Indian culture, explaining how a focus on a glorious past defines their spiritual life. The author notes that the Indian people view the future as gloomy, leading even the young to dwell on the antiquity and marvels of the world's creation.</summary>
<keywords>Indian lore, Mongolian ancestor, antiquity, Corn Priests, Guardians of the Seed, Dragonfly, Zuni philosophy, cultural heritage</keywords>

<sig>VIII</sig>

the outermost borders of his native range, he turns his back to the coming storm and with sullen serenity awaits it; musing, meanwhile, on the scenes of other days and the tales of other generations. In tune with the wild winds of the mesas and mountains where he roams and watches over his herds, he composes the music of his songs—songs which are but the echoes of words uttered generations before the white man knew him. All the genius of his best birthrights—his imaginative mind and picturesquely poetic language—he devotes to the beautification of ancient wonder-tales, so that he may teach his little ones, whom he dearly loves, to emulate him in seeking joy in the memories of a dead but known past, rather than in the hopes of a living but unknown future. Alone with his family at night, while the winter wind shrieks outside and the piñon light dances within, you would not think him a mournful being. His fingers are stretched out, his eyes gleaming, and his whole manner joyful and spirited, as he recounts the adventures of his ancestors with gods, monsters, and

Very long, long ago, the old ruined village of *Ha'-wi-k'uh* was filled with the fathers of our ancestors, as were many towns all around it that are also ruined now. The plains below were covered with the fertile washes of spring streams, and the mists from the hot springs above drove away the breath of the Ice God, so that the cold never grew severe in the valley. Thus it happened that year after year more corn grew for the people of *Ha'-wi-k'uh* than they needed, and they became rich and arrogant with their abundance.

One day, the Chief Priest of the Bow saw some children playing at mock warfare, using dirt and lumps of mud as their weapons. “Aha!” he mused, “I will devise a way to delight my people and show the nations all around that our wealth and good fortune are greater than theirs!”

No one thanked her for her offerings; yet many beings lived by her bounty, for instead of throwing away the scraps of her food, she fed hungry dogs with them, and threw them away so that the snowbirds and chickadees might pick them up.

When, long before the winter was over, the old and young began to die, what was to be done? The chiefs and priests called a council. A delegation of the strongest men was sent away to the country of the Moquis. <note>11</note> After many days, two runners from Moqui, strong and hearty, arrived at the village. One night, the creature in the cage flew away. He did not come back the next morning; only his cage hung there, and the corn he had dropped was nearly gone. He flew south past many mountains and plains, as straight as a drawn bowstring, to the Land of Everlasting Summer. There were green trees everywhere; everywhere flowers were blooming and fruits were always ripening in that far-off Summerland. Birds and butterflies lived there, and in the valley of a great forest lived the Corn Maidens. As he neared their home, he rested, for his flight had been long, and he did not know where to find the maidens. So, wherever a corn plant grew, he settled on its tassels, then flew to another, and another, until at last he reached the home of the Corn Maidens. The two sisters who had lived for a time in the grotto of the White Cliffs were walking through the great cornfields when they heard the creature buzzing.

When he saw the two little ones sitting under the window, bright and healthy, his joy knew no bounds, and he rushed eagerly up to them, exclaiming:

“Ah, my beloved little ones, is it possible, is it possible that I see you, and have you been happy these many days?” But to his surprise they never smiled, nor spoke to him, and seemed scarcely to know of his presence. “My beloved little ones,” he said, going and bending over them until his gray hair almost touched them, “do you not know that I am your old uncle?” Still they did not reply, nor did they smile.

He raised himself sorrowfully and looked about the room. It was as bare as when the people had departed for Moqui; except that it was clean and well-ordered, there was no difference. No trace of food nor the leftovers of meals met his eye.

“Poor little creatures!” he thought in his heart. “I will offer them food; perhaps they have lived as prairie dogs do in winter—sleeping; who knows?”

The old man looked around the room again. There was no fuel near the hearthstone, except for a few twigs. > “At least I may stay with you for three or four days, and I will gather wood in the meantime so that you do not suffer from the cold. I cannot stay permanently, for my provisions—though I offer them freely to my sister’s children—are meager, and the journey from here is long.”

This time the little boy bowed his head and smiled, and the old uncle was greatly gladdened.

> "I will paint your form in remembrance on the sacred things, emblematic of spring and the health-giving rains of springtime; and I shall paint your companion, the symbol of summer and the pools of summer showers."

The Dragon-fly poised for a moment in the air over the boy's head, then like a "star seeking the house of a wife" <note>meteor</note>, he sped forth over the broad cornfields.

Therefore, to this day, the dragon-fly (the black, white, and red one) comes in early summer when the corn tassels bloom, humming from one plant to another, yet never content with his resting place.

And following him comes the beautiful green dragon-fly; for the boy made the companion of the first dragon-fly out of the green stalks of corn, and so the green dragon-fly is green with yellow light, like a stalk of growing corn in the sunlight.

## CHAPTER III

### LAND LAW AND LABOR

<image-desc>A line drawing of a tall, square-shaped monolith or boundary stone decorated with carvings and geometric patterns, standing in a desolate or desert landscape with hills in the background. No branch of the industrial arts of the Zuñi Indians is shown as clearly as in their farming customs and methods: first, the influences of the climatic environment on a people’s religion and culture, and then the effects of this belief and philosophy on their daily life. Before examining these interesting topics, however, a significant, but I hope not tiresome, digression must be made to provide some idea of the land laws of primitive Pueblodom.

The Zuñi tribe today (I shall speak of it frequently as a nation, for it is the remnant of such) includes only between sixteen and seventeen hundred members. This population is divided, first, into six subtribes, each taking its name from the *ki'-wi-tsin*, or sacred house, to which it belongs. Again, without reference to this plan of subdivision, the tribe contains thirteen organizations, orders, or sacred societies, founded upon four primary elements in savage life: war, hunting, the priesthood, and the medical fraternities.

Yet again, owing allegiance to neither of the preceding, is a third subdivision into the farming tribes, which derive their names from the summer pueblos near which their principal fields are located. The names of these geographic tribes are, in order of precedence, three: *Tâ'-ia-kwe*, "People of the Planting Town"; *He-sho-ta-tsi'-na-kwe*, "People of the Pictured Town" (from the sculptured pictograms on the foundation walls of their village); and the

More important than any of the preceding in its relation to the tenure of corn-land is the kinship subdivision, for there are, regardless of these others, sixteen clans. In order of their rank, they are named as follows:<sup>14</sup> The Parrot or Macaw people, the Corn or Seed, the Badger, Sun, Eagle, Turkey, Crane, Deer, Bear, Coyote, Frog, Grouse, Tobacco, Spring-vine (or Chick-weed), Yellow-wood, and Rattlesnake peoples. 

The Parrot and Seed clans are nearly equal in membership, each containing about three hundred members. From these, the numbers decrease throughout the other clans down to five of the Yellow-wood people, and only one living representative of the Rattlesnake clan—a man with whom, of course, the clan will end. Thus, it may be seen that one small nation is organized on four different principles, none of which has any dependency on the others, except in their religious aspect: (1) The sacred government, according to the places of worship; (2) the secular government, according to landed and water

If this paper were treating the sociology rather than the food production of the Zuñis, I could show how these four kinds of subdivisions harmonize with one another; how, indeed, the first three were the outgrowth of the fundamental social principle of the tribe, and how, finally, with the addition of the phratral combinations of clans (now modified or outgrown among the Zuñis), all four features were nearly universal to aboriginal America. As it is, I must confine further remarks to what these things seem to tell us of pre-Columbian Pueblo life, and to a discussion of the relation they bear to the land, water, and food possessions of the tribe.

Although the early Spaniards undoubtedly exaggerated the population of Cibola (more through imperfect methods of gathering data than from willfulness) in stating it was as great as "eleven thousand souls," we may safely conclude from a calculation of the rooms in the six ruins named above, that altogether they and ancient Zuñi contained more than six thousand inhabitants.<note>17</note> This seems only reasonable when we study the immense stock of lore, ritual, and ceremony of the tribe, and, more than anything else, the elaborate and highly differentiated organizations mentioned above. All these point not to a vast or dense population, but still to a very numerous and quite highly yet naturally developed ancestry.

When, during the years of the Pueblo rebellion (1680 to 1692), the Zuñis sought to fortify themselves against Spanish vengeance on the Rock Mountain of Thunder,<note>18</note>

On the top of the Mountain of Thunder they built their town, not all together but in six different blocks or terraced masses, each mass representing one of the abandoned towns. This was significant. Great error has always been committed in considering the Indians, particularly the Pueblos, as (in our sense of the word) communists. Not even among ourselves is the division of property or individual land-tenure carried further. It is in consequence of a native method of speaking, law, or custom regulating the disposal of land that these curious people have come to be regarded as property communists.

Suppose that a young man belongs to the Parrot clan; he cannot marry any girl, however remote her relationship to him may be, who belongs to the same clan. As descent is on the mother’s side, his children do not belong to him nor to his clan, but to his wife and her clan. If he, either before or after his marriage, “raises the sand” (takes up or clears a field), it belongs strictly

The procedure by which a Zuñi seeks to bequeath lands that he has inherited or reclaimed is curious. Nominally, as explained above, such lands belong to his clan. In bestowing them upon his children—by which, of course, he transfers them to his wife's clan—he must, in the absence of any writing, make arrangements within whichever of the thirteen secret organizations of sacred medicine (*<term>ti-kĭtla-pon</term>*, or *<term>ti'-kia</term>*) he belongs to. In the presence of the council of this society, he states with great detail all the particulars of his bequest. Years may pass. However, none of his items are revealed, unless by himself, until after his death. If any question then arises, the members who listened to his declaration, acting as witnesses to one another, reveal what the will of the deceased was. As an illustration of their process, nothing could be more interesting or instructive than an account of a lawsuit at which, as (at the

One evening in the autumn of 1881, my older brother, Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa, the head chief, said to me:

"Younger brother, wash your eyes in cold water."

"Why?"

"An old beast who belongs to the clan of the man who was his uncle wishes to take a peach orchard away from his brothers <note>cousins</note>, the children of the deceased."

Soon after, I heard the herald call out a council from the distant housetops.

The old man had just finished stuffing the big black throat of the family hearth with piñon sticks when the members of the upcoming council began to slip in. Each was wrapped from nose to instep in his blanket; each, moreover, was as grave and dignified as any senator in history. From the depths of each blanket, as the threshold was crossed, the invariable greeting would issue: "How are you these many days?" to which the response was given expressionlessly, *Kets'-in-i-shi; i-ti-ni-k'ia!*—"Happy; gather

Sheepskins, dogskins, buffalo robes, discarded blankets, four-legged stools, bundles of corn husks, and long slender rolls of dry cedar bark were scattered across the floor, and a bag or two of hard old plug tobacco lay in the firelight. As the council members gathered, everything except the husks, cedar rolls, and tobacco was taken as a seat. No sooner had they sat than the room sounded like a hailstorm on dry fodder—a sound caused by the rustling of corn husks—for everyone who sat down (and none remained standing) immediately grabbed at the pile of husks and began to cut out a piece with his thumbnail, of a length suitable to serve as a cigarette wrapper. Once cut, the husk was moistened with the tongue and scraped with the teeth until it reached the proper state of thinness and flexibility. It was then neatly rolled into the shape of the intended cigarette and tucked into the top of a legging to hold its form. Meanwhile, a small piece of the dried plug tobacco was attacked with the

The second chief is at the same time sergeant-at-arms and justice, or, more precisely, secretary. In the former capacity, he has to rage and swear and thump the floor with his staff, jumping up, sitting down, and expressing ferocious wrath in his every action, but keeping his heart as unperturbed as a <term>Hindoo rishi's</term> during penance.

In the second capacity, he has to listen intently. This is done with a view toward straining twenty-five minutes of serious, significant statements of fact out of five to seven midnight hours of vituperative recrimination and violent personal abuse. This abuse does not hesitate to rake up from the traditional tribal annals every scandal, calumny, and other vicious bit of back-biting contained within at least two ancestral generations of the parties "mentioned in the council." account. Regarding lands, water rights, and the trespassing of animals and children, lawsuits are the order of the day (or rather, night) every autumn. Since they are all conducted in much the same way, this description of one will represent the many that must be mentioned later. Moreover, the legal custom regulating the transfer of land by inheritance from one clan to another has a fair, though only partial, illustration in the example above.

When a young <term>Zuñi</term> wishes to increase his land holdings, he travels across the country, seemingly unconcerned about the distance. He selects the mouth of an <term>arroyo</term> (a deep, dry gully or stream-course) that winds from the plain into the hills or mountains; finding a flat stretch of ground where it merges into the plain, his first task is to “lift the sand.” This is done by striking the hoe into the earth at intervals of five or six yards and pulling out small heaps of soil until a line of tiny boundary mounds has been formed around the proposed field. Next, within this space, he cuts away the sagebrush—

He then builds up long banks of sand along the line first indicated by the heaps of soil. Each embankment is called a *<term>so'-pit-thlan</term>* ("sand string"). At every corner he places a rock—if possible, a columnar one—sometimes roughly sculpted with his tokens <note>this refers to an illustration at the beginning of the original text</note>.

It is rare for him to do anything more to the plot in a single year. Not infrequently, even years before the land is actually required for cultivation, the "sand is lifted" and a stone of a distinctive shape is placed at one corner as a mark of ownership. From then on, unless it is surrendered, the place remains the exclusive property of the one who lifted the sand, or, in the event of his death, of the clan to which he belonged.

While riding across the ancient country of the <term>Zuñis</term>, I have sometimes found these rows of small soil heaps as far as forty miles away from the central valley. Distance could not have been the sole cause for the abandonment of these plots, as some fields, still under the hoe, are just as far away; yet they give evidence of having been cultivated, probably because of great fertility, for several generations.

With the Zuñis, one-half the months in the year are “nameless,” and the others are “named.” The year is called “a passage of time,” the seasons “the steps” (of the year), and the months “crescents”—probably because each begins with the new moon. New Year is called the “Mid-journey of the sun;” that is, the middle of the solar trip between one summer solstice and another, and, occurring invariably about the nineteenth of December, it usually initiates a short season of great religious activity. The first month after this is now called *<term>I’-koh-pu-yä-tchun</term>*, “Growing white crescent,” as with it begins the Southwestern winter—the origin of the name is

The ancient name of the month seems to have had a different meaning, although it sounded strikingly similar: *I-shoh-k'o'a-pu-yä-tchun* or “Crescent of the conception.” This is undoubtedly a reference to the kindling of the sacred fire by drilling with an arrow shaft into a piece of soft, dry wood root, a ceremony that is still strictly observed. Interesting evidence of this meaning can be found on the tribe's old notched calendar sticks, where the first month of the new year is indicated by a small fire socket at one end.

The second month is *Ta'-yäm-tchu-yä-tchun*, so named because it is the time when boughs are broken by the weight of falling snow.

Then follows *O-nan-ul'-ak-k'ia-kwum-yä-tchun*, or the month during which “snow does not lie in the pathways,” which ends winter, or the “Sway of cold.”

Spring, called the “Starting time,” opens with *Thli'-te-kwa-na-k'ia-tsa-na-yä-tchun*, or the month of the “Lesser sandstorms,” followed by *Thli'-te-kwa-na-k'ia-thla'-na-yä-tchun*, or the month of the “Greater sandstorms,” and this—the ugliest season of the

Zuñi year, is closed by *Yä-tchun-kwa-shi'-am-o-na*, the "Crescent of no name." Summer and autumn, the period of the "nameless months," are together called *O'-lo-i-k'ia*, the season "Bringing flour-like clouds." In priestly or ritualistic language these six months, although called nameless, are designated successively the "yellow, blue, red, white, variegated or iridescent, and black," after the colors of the plumed prayer-sticks sacrificed in rotation at the full of each moon to the gods of the north, west, south, east, the skies, and the lower regions respectively.

In common speech, these months and the minute divisions of the seasons they embrace, are referred to by terms descriptive of the growth of corn plants and the development and ripening of their grain. There will be, on a future page, an occasion to illustrate the tendency of the Zuñis to make corn the standard of measurement and comparison not only for time, but for many other things, by the reproduction of a unique song of one of the sacred orders.

Early in the month of the “Lesser sand-storms,” the same Zuñi who, for example, claimed a distant arroyo-field a year ago, goes out with a hoe and axe in hand to resume the work of clearing, etc. Within the sand embankment, he now selects that portion where the arroyo enters from above; cutting many forked cedar branches, he drives them firmly into the dry stream-bed in a line crossing its course and extending a considerable distance beyond either bank. Against this row of stakes, he places boughs, clods, rocks, sticks, and earth, so as to form a strong barrier or dry-dam; it is left open, however, at either end. A few rods <note>A rod is a unit of measurement equal to 16.5 feet or 5.5 yards.</note> below this on either side of the stream's course, he constructs other and longer barriers less carefully. Still further down, he looks in the “tracks” of some past torrent for a ball of clay which, having been detached from its native bank far above, has been rolled and washed down and down—continually growing rounder, smaller, and tougher—until it lies embedded in and baked by the burning sands in these lower plains. is considered the winning side. This race is usually run by no fewer than twelve men, with six players against an equal number. The distance normally covered without rest or even slowing down is twenty-five miles. Now, the time taken in running this race is remarkably short, never exceeding three hours; yet, if you were to ask one of the runners to undertake the race without his stick, he would flatly tell you he could not possibly do it. The Zuñis are so convinced of this idea that frequently, when coming in from distant fields and wishing to make haste, they cut a stick and kick it ahead of them, running to catch up with it, and so on. The interesting feature about all this is that the Indian in this, as in most other things, confuses the cause with the effect, thinking the stick helps him instead of himself being the sole driving force of the stick. The lump of clay mentioned before is supposed to be the *ti'-kwa* of the water gods, fashioned by their invisible hands and pushed along by their irresistible feet—not slowing down, but adding to the force and speed of the waters. At the stage of operations just described, the field is left again for a year so that it may become thoroughly enriched. Meanwhile, during the same month (the first of spring), each planter repairs the banks in his old fields and proceeds to adopt a completely different method for renewing or enriching the soil.

Along the western sides of his field, as well as in any spots throughout it that are worn out or barren, he thickly plants rows of sagebrush, leaving them standing from six inches to a foot above the surface. Since the prevailing winds of the <term>Zuñi</term> plains come from the southwest, and since during the following month (the “Crescent of the greater sandstorms”), these winds are filled many tens of feet into the air with fine dust and sand, a long, level, and deep deposit of soil drifts behind each row of sagebrush. "Father and Mother of Corn-crops" or
seed; the <term>yä'-po-to</term> being the "male," and the
<term>mi'-k'iap-pan-ne</term> being the "female."

As she nears the tray, she says, over the objects in her hands (addressing the new corn), “My children, how have you been these many days?” Then the new corn is supposed to reply through the voices of the other women, now gathered nearby, “Happily, our elders; happily!” With this, the corn matron deposits her burden on the new bunch of soot, and all present say short prayers significant of the occasion and setting forth their wishes for “long life, happy fortune, and the health of strength born of the food of maize.” This ceremony is called the “Meeting of the Children,” and is performed in commemoration of the return of the lost Corn Maidens under the guidance of Pai'-a-tu-ma, and their welcome by the Seed priests of ancient Zuñi.

When all the harvest has been gathered, dried, sorted, and stacked up around and over the "father and mother" in the corn room, the ceremony that was interrupted at the beginning is resumed. Reverently—for she is in the presence of the conscious and the benign, or so it seems to her—she approaches the stack of corn and with her left hand takes from the selected ears along the top, one ear for each finger (that is, four); then with her right hand, she takes an equal number, placing them in the tray. She brings these forth and, assisted by the male head of the household, shells them with such care that not a single kernel is lost. Dust from the old bunch of soot is scattered over the shelled corn, and a curious sacred pigment is prepared in an earthen ladle, made of yellow paint and a grain of salt from the mountain near the Lake of the Dead and the Salt Lake in the south. To these ingredients are added two or three kinds of little yellow flowers, the principal variety being precious in the eyes of the Zuñi as that which was “left over from the seed stores of the gods.” All this is mixed with pollen and water, and the entire tray of kernels is thoroughly sprinkled and anointed by stirring. All this is done so that the "seed" may have the power of reproduction, rapid growth, and strength, and that it may bear fruit possessing the properties of food—fruit that shall mature during the season when the little yellow flowers thrive and bloom most: early autumn. We are at first surprised when we learn that the corn treated in this way has a remarkable degree of vigor and the quality of ripening early; but our wonder may be lessened when we reflect that these seeds are the most perfect of the entire harvest, selected mostly from those ears which reached maturity soonest. Still, to the Zuñi, all these things are living testaments of faith, proving the infallibility of his theory of "medicine," or <term>fetishism</term>, and of his practice of religion.

The corn, now fully prepared, is poured into a pouch made from the whole skin of a fawn (pl. III, *b*). Most fantastic in appearance is this spotted, life-like corn-bag as it hangs at night against the wall, gilded by the firelight, head downward, with the incessantly flickering shadows of its broad ears

I have told how, during the months of the sand-storms, the banks in the old corn-fields are newly built up. Little more needs to be done, and on some fine morning in May, the voice—low, mournful, yet strangely penetrating and tuneful—of the Sun Priest is heard from the housetops. As you listen in the shadow of some tall terrace, you think that voice must come from a spirit of the heroic age of Zuñi, returned on the night-wind and hastening to call his wayward, game-obsessed children to the fields; so old-fashioned and so hidden in meaning seem the words it is uttering. III, *c*) is a kind of prod made from a straight-grained juniper sapling, its base flattened and sharpened to a round-nosed, blade-like point, and featuring one "ear" formed by a natural branch cut off and scraped until just enough is left to be useful as a brace for the right foot.

The tool our friend has just finished sharpening glistens from long use. The blade is worn short, ground shorter, and the whole thing has an air of antiquity; it was, likely as not, made long ago by the man’s grandfather on the mother’s side or by some other equally early tinkerer in the beginning of this century or late in the last. He will not use this venerable relic, let us hope, for planting the whole field; but at any rate, he prefers it, short though it be, for the work currently at hand. At the end of the fourth day after the first planting, the householder quite likely makes a new planting-stick (pl. III, *d*), laying the old one aside. He also gets out his seed bags. These (pl. III, *e*) are curious. Usually made of rawhide, they have been so puckered and sewn that they form egg-shaped containers, cut off at the smaller end. They are ingeniously made to remain open and otherwise retain their shape by being moistened, filled first with damp, then with moderately hot, dry sand, and hung up to harden by desiccation, which of course takes place in a short time. A little hoop of wood is, moreover, fitted around the upper edge, much like the large wire rim of a tin bucket, and, like the latter, the seed-pouch is also furnished with a handle <note>bail</note>—made of twisted buckskin.

181

staggering under a big earthen canteen of water, the planter now proceeds to his field. Along the eastern side of the rows of last year’s broken stalks (or corn butts), four or five inches from each bunch, he digs holes with his wooden prod to a depth of four to seven inches. The boy follows after him, dropping twelve to twenty kernels into each hole and pushing sand in with his foot until it is filled. Wherever the stalk-butts happen to be thin, they reinforce them with bunches of greasewood or sagebrush sprigs. The result is that not only is the crop not planted twice in succession in the same spots, but a long drift of fresh soil is blown by the still prevailing west winds directly over each new hill of corn, forming, without labor, neat little mounds of earth. The country of the Zuñi is so dry that the seeds have to be planted at great depths—even at the cost of a significant delay in their growth—and the little drifts of sandy soil protect the underlying loam in which the kernels are embedded from the fierce southwestern sun. Not only because of this dryness,

   Now comes the time when the young Zuñi and his elder brother may indulge in fanciful creations that would astound the most talented scarecrow makers of New England. The glossy, large, Southwestern crow or raven is abroad. He sits on every rock, soars through every cloud-shadow, and laughs and cackles in every corn arroyo at safe, yet impertinent, distances from the busy planter. He as much as says to his companions in the language of Zuñi crow lore: “Ah! You must wait until those little green spikes come up! They grow solely for our benefit, so that we may have signs to find the good things those long-legged, fearful fellows are hiding so deep in the sand. Why, that’s what our heavy noses are provided for!” Alas, poor birds! Have they forgotten last season? What a shock is in store for them! What disappointment, which will soon be attested by the most discordant caw-croaks of anguish!

The old man is busy setting up cedar poles at intervals of a few rods all over the field. Not knowing what these poles were for, you would think an eastern bean-patch or hop-field had been moved to Zuñiland. But if you look carefully, you will see that each pole is topped with a bunch of its own or some other prickly leaves so that the crows cannot land on it. Moreover, the busy planter is now stringing cords of split yucca leaves from one pole to another; because they are so numerous, they would remind you of the telegraph wires of New York City if they were not so knotty. A kind of network is thus formed all over the field. To make this more impressive, tattered rags, pieces of dog and coyote skins, old shoulder blades tied in groups of two or three, streamers of moss—in fact, streamers of every conceivable thing that has the quality of swaying in the wind—are thickly attached to these many cords. This makes them look much as I imagine a clothesline would after being hit by a hurricane (pl. iv).

Meanwhile, the youngsters are busy.

They have pilfered from the old storeroom every piece of discarded clothing they could lay their hands on. You must know, my reader, that this is exactly what their fathers and uncles want; but it is not so for their mothers, aunts, and grandmothers. These representatives of Zuñi <term>consanguinity</term> <note>kinship or blood relation</note> are the stingiest creatures to whom human breath was ever granted. If a dress is too dirty and ragged to be worn comfortably, it will serve—when backed by straw—to plug up <term>sky-holes</term> <note>smoke-holes or roof openings</note>; if it is too worn out for this, it is still useful as baby bedding; and furthermore, if it is not even good enough for that, it is highly valued in their eyes for the manufacture of "holders of hot things" <note>pot holders</note>. Therefore, it is stored away along with numerous predecessors for the "wanting time" <note>time of need</note>. Yet, a young Zuñi is just as sharp as any other boy. He gets what he desires, rest assured, and he does so without the knowledge of even his younger sister. Off to the deep <term>arroyo</term> <note>a dry creek bed or gulch</note> near his father's field he goes with his plunder. His older brother is "in on it" with him. Both of them have been deprived all their lives of slates and pencils.

# CORN-RAISING

They have found no outlet for their great talent for caricature, and they express it on occasions like this. They are highly inventive, bold, and quick to act. Twenty-four hours from now, look at the result! As you ride along a trail leading out of town, your feelings would be joyful if it were not for the effect on your unsteady Indian horse. He cannot be convinced that those things standing or sitting around so often are lifeless!

Over yonder on the hillside is an old woman limping (*but not moving along*). She carries a basket on her back and a rattle made of a rib, a shoulder blade <note>scapula</note>, a tin can, and a stick in her hand. Does it rattle? Yes; it is safe to say that you can hear it if the wind is blowing, even before you see the stuffed old woman. Not so with the new generation of "kernel diggers," which grows feathers and finds wings about this time. Before growth has made the corn invulnerable, these guileless young creatures come along. They are no more fearful of the extravagant effigies than of the embracing branches of their paternal nesting place <note>paternal rookery</note>. Many of them, therefore, get caught in little hair nooses attached in abundance to convenient stones <note>cobbles</note>. Others commit suicide in pairs by swallowing the tempting kernels at either end of a hair thread and then winding one another up and choking. They seem to prefer this to being "Siamese twins" all their lives!

Of course, the wretched birds "die young" and are then fastened to two flexible twigs and hung, head downward, from one of the many yucca lines. This course of action is, it seems, prompted by the belief that the souls of these dead crows will warn their living companions that man is "very painful," and so that these souls may not lack witnesses, they are provided with their own bodies, hung up in conspicuous places.<sup>21</sup>

The scarecrow and the bird it scares are subjects of such serious interest to the Zuñi, such a source of agitation during its brief season in his agricultural life, and so clearly the primary cause of trouble for his grain (a subject about which he is as sensitive as a miser), that a small anecdote regarding the bird in particular seems to me to be appropriate.

That his neighbors' scarecrows were better than his own was not in itself an aggravation, but it was certainly a nuisance, for it caused the crows to leave their fields and actually flock to his. He came to my "little house" one morning, looking weary.

"What is on your mind?" I asked.

"Crows!"

"Why don't you make scarecrows?" I said.

"Scarecrows? Ha! Nothing will remedy the folly of our ancestors; nothing, I say, younger brother!"

"Why? What did they do?" I asked, reaching for a pencil.

"Now, look here!" exclaimed the old man. "You little fool, put away that writing stick. I am very serious this morning, and I want to ask you two questions."

## CHAPTER V

### CORN-RAISING, OR "THE REGENERATION OF THE SEED"

<image-desc>A rectangular line-art illustration featuring two burros (donkeys) with their heads appearing among stalks of corn. On the left side of the image, a large, ornate letter "W" is integrated into the drawing, serving as the drop-cap initial for the first word of the text.</image-desc>

WHEN the kernels have sprouted all through the field described in the last chapter, we find the planter busy inspecting the hills near the prayer-stick. Upon this inspection hangs the fate, so *he* thinks, of his cornfield; for if every kernel in each of the six sacred hills has "come out," the crop will be productive. If, on the contrary, one or two of the grains in, for example, the southern hill, have not sprouted forth, Alas! part of his crop of red corn will be a failure—it will not get ripe before frost time.

dren of the household, and perhaps by as many neighbors. Wherever a sprout looks yellow, they dig down and kill the little white worm they are sure to find near the root. This is called "grub-finishing." Wherever the plants are very vigorous, they pull up all except four or five of the best, and this is called "leafing," or "leaf-lifting."

The occasion which follows soon and is recurrent twice or thrice during the warm season, is perhaps the jolliest of the summer. It is the "hoeing" or "staving time," as the Zuñis call it in clear remembrance of the instruments with which their ancestors hoed, away back in the Stone Age. These were crooked, sharp-edged staves of hard wood, shaped not unlike sickles, or better still, short scythes (pl. III, *f*). Rude as they were, they seem to have been wonderfully effective in the removal of weeds, for the worker, progressing on his knees, swept the scythe-hoe from side to side between the rows of corn, cutting off wide swaths of weeds, just below the surface of the soft, yielding soil. Laughing, joking, telling stories of the olden times (*not folklore, as that is forbidden while the rattlesnake is out!*), racing at their task, and playing pranks, they are the most light-hearted laborers you have ever seen.

According to these stories, it was not like this in the olden times of which they tell. Armed even while they worked, brave with desperation, it was rare that they ever saw Zuñi again; for the cowardly Navajos rarely came except in swarms. Some of the most thrilling traditions in the Zuñi language concern these events and the harvest days of long ago; and it is with regret that I pass by my notes of many a long recital for the short and perhaps less interesting tale below.

But it has been fifty years since the flames died away on that hearthstone; for fifty years a little streak of sunlight has played along the blanket-pole, replacing the fire’s ruddy glow; and for fifty years the story has been told at each hoeing of how the woman went out one morning, never to return.

For the little house on the rock once belonged to <term>Um'-thla-na</term>, “He-Of-Large-Muscles.” He was living there with his family to tend the cornfields. The women went out early one morning to get water. No sooner had they neared the distant pool than they heard the sound of many horses' hooves. Then they saw, sweeping down the valley, a crowd of mounted warriors. They dropped their water jars and fled—one to the neighboring rocks, appearing hours later, breathless and fainting, at Zuñi; but the younger fled toward the little tower, the steps of which she never climbed; for, caught up by some wrangling horsemen fighting over her, she was carried away into years of captivity.

Um'-thla-na heard the rush of the riders. He grabbed his war club, bow, and arrows, and without pausing to close the doorway, he climbed the step-log in the corner and barricaded the trapdoor. Soon the Navahos swarmed into the lower room. They snatched the serapes from the blanket pole and stole the basket of corn cakes and paper bread. Wild with joy over these delicacies, which were so rare in their nomadic life, they never noticed the trapdoor, but ran out and sat down around the doorway to feast.

Alas, Um'-thla-na! Why did he not stay quiet? Peering out through a porthole, he saw a large Navaho calmly sitting near the step-log, eating a roll of paper bread. He drew an arrow back to its head, let it fly, and struck the feasting raider so squarely that the man never uttered a groan, but fell over against the ladder, still clutching his roll of *guayave*. Another man, sitting nearby, saw him fall, but before he could raise an alarm, he too was pinned by one of Um'-thla-na's arrows. As this one fell, Um'-thla-na raised a shout of victory, "changing his voice so that the Navahos might think there were many of him."

<gloss>Um'-thla-na: He-Of-Large-Muscles; Navahos: Navajo people; serapes: blanket-like shawls; paper-bread: a thin, wafer-like corn bread (also known as guayave); guayave: paper-bread; Zuni: a Pueblo tribe.</gloss>

At first the enemy fell back, but when they found there was only one man, they rushed toward the house again. For a while Um'-thla-na's arrows fell so thickly that the danger of approaching closely kept the Navahos from charging. Even when his arrows were spent, he pulled stones from the wall and broke them against one another, throwing them down at the enemy. The portholes were small, and he had to stand quite close to them. Soon an arrow whizzed through one, piercing him in the arm. Um'-thla-na clenched his teeth and plucked it out, shooting it back.

Before long he was wounded in many places and weak from loss of blood; still, he stood bravely at bay by the portholes. One of the Navahos, further away than the rest, saw Um'-thla-na's face at the hole. Taking careful aim, he released his arrow so skillfully that Um'-thla-na, while dodging, was shot through the neck. He staggered back, falling heavily, then roused himself and sat up against the wall, clutching his war club. *Now the Navahos rushed toward the doorway. Suddenly they fled away, for, be-*

<header>ZUÑI BREADSTUFF</header>
<sig>VIII</sig>

Look! Coming swiftly across the valley in a cloud of dust was a band of Zuñi horsemen. The Zuñis pursued the fleeing Navahos, never thinking of Um'-thla-na. At last the poor old man, hearing no sound, pulled some of the arrows from his wounds, broke others off, and slowly, painfully clambered down the step-log and staggered out into the plain toward Zuñi. Fainter and fainter he grew until he fainted by the trail side. Toward sunset they found him there—those who came to search. Some stayed to tenderly care for him, while others went to search for the young woman. They did not find *her*, but lying dead on the rocks near the tower were five Navahos. One of them was leaning against the step-log, still grasping in his hand a roll of paper-bread. Um'-thla-na lived to tell the story, but grew worse as the arrow wounds festered, and "killed himself so that he might be separated from pain."

Nobody lives in the little house now. "It is a place of painful thoughts," say the narrators; but it stands always the same, for its builder was He-Of-Large-Muscles.

At sunset, the men file in from the field. The women have spread, or rather, strung the feast out on the lowest roof. Ten or twelve great bowls sit in a row, smoking hot with stew, every one as red with <term>chile</term> as its rising vapors are with the colors of the sunset. There is a row of <term>breadstuff</term>, thin as paper and flaky as crackers—red, yellow, blue, and white—piled up in baskets down either side of the meat bowls. Outside these are two other rows, this time made of blankets and stool blocks. The first man whose head appears up the ladder is besieged with polite invitations to "Sit and eat; sit and eat," from as many pairs of lips as there are women on the housetop. When all are seated, a sacrifice is made to the household fire. Up to this time, the talking has been frequent; now it ceases altogether. Everything except eating seems <term>tabu</term> until the feast has disappeared and the cigarettes are rolled and lit. Then talking resumes and continues long into the night.

Autumn comes and the "corn children" have been taken in to meet their "father and mother," the <term>yä'-po-to</term> and the <term>mi'-k'iap-pan-ne</term>. At the top, it is cut wider around to a depth of a foot or more and walled up neatly and solidly with sandstone. Below this wall—say, a foot down—the hole is gradually enlarged toward the bottom until it forms a room several feet in diameter and cone-shaped, with the apex being the walled, circular opening. <header>ZUÑI BREADSTUFF</header>

late next morning. At last, the embers have burned low, and smoke has stopped rising from their glaring red depths. Green and plentiful cornstalks are thrown in, more are tucked into the large draft-hole, and preparations are made for artificially ripening that which nature has delayed. A beautiful, long, fresh stalk is chosen, complete with leaves, tassels, and roots. Two fine ears of corn are stripped of their husks. One of them is laid against the stalk; the other is cleaned of its silk as if for boiling. The chief of ceremonials bites off all the milky kernels from this, mouthful by mouthful, chews them to a pulp, and blows their substance in a fine mist over the heaps of plucked corn. He then places the cob by the side of the other ear and binds both firmly to the stalk. This, in the brief prayer he soon makes, is called the *shi'-wa-ni*, or priest. It is thrown into the still-glowing pit, and then men and women, young and old, begin to hurl in the unhusked corn from all sides until no more is left. Most likely, space remains at the top.

A mound of damp soil is heaped to a considerable height above this impromptu stopper. As night again comes on, campfires—bright enough, it is true, but pale compared with the flames of last night—are built at convenient distances. Muffled sounds come all night from the buried oven. Sometimes, though rarely, the top is blown off, but usually next morning the mound is found unchanged and the sounds have ceased.

Now comes a sight which would surprise a stranger, even if he were miles away. The earthen mound is removed and the stopper of cornstalks is, with great trepidation, most gingerly pulled out. Instantly, hissing and seething, the steam from the heated corn and stalks below shoots hundreds of feet into the air. Every member of the party, as they approach Zuñi, may be seen gorging on this really delicious baked corn. When it is unloaded into the spare room, the heat has not yet left it. With all possible haste, the husks are stripped down, and the ears, now brown and plump, are braided into long bunches, and the whole lot is hung up to dry in an upper room.

Many of the leaves in the field still remain green. These are gathered, carefully dried, and folded into large, long bundles for winter kitchen use. Quantities of late squash and pumpkin flowers are stored away in jars to serve a similar purpose.

In fact, had he been able to run, he would certainly have done so at the sight of a field of corn.

Out of pity for both crows and burros, I have sometimes pleaded for a lessening of the customary harsh measures. My experiences at such times lead me to advise all aspiring ethnologists to mind their own business when corn is the subject. As I have said before, the Zuñis, and probably most other Indians, are sensitive on the subject of their staple food.

Frost arrives, changing the green of the stalks to yellow gold and the leaf-like husks to feathers. In every field, there are corn pickers and huskers. Any corn that is not husked in the field is packed with great skill on burros or in carts and a few second-hand wagons, and brought to the town. Husking bees are formed by the women, and at three o’clock any afternoon, you can see mountains of discarded husks around a corner, and many a black, frizzy head sticking up from their flaky slopes, bobbing as if without a body with the severing of every ear from its rattling wrappings. At such times, husks in great numbers are selected, bundled into neat bunches, and strung several feet long on threads of yucca fiber. They will be needed before the month is over, particularly in the council chambers, where every night brings the weary lawgivers of Zuñi fresh cases of trespass for consideration.

How the roofs groan under the weight of drying corn; how the walls gleam and glow with festoons of chile or red pepper! (pl. VII). But in time the corn is dry, the peppers are ripened enough for storage, and the work of “corn-sorting” begins. The different colors—yellow, blue, red, white, speckled, and black—are separated. The “nubbin-ears” (small, stunted ears) are put in a cellar by themselves for sale or for burros, and, as described before, the corn is stacked up in the granary around the tutelar divinities of the place—the “Father and Mother of corn crops.”

<header>CORN-RAISING</header>

### XIII

->*Sa-ni-hi'-akia, thla-shi-nai-ye.*<-
->Band of hunters, their corn grown aged.<-

This song, although beautiful in the original language and music (possessing as it does perfect meter, fine rhythm, and significant poetic sentiment), defies exact translation. Not only is it composed of archaic syllables, but the terms in Zuñi for every phenomenon connected with corn and its growth are so numerous and technical that it is as difficult to translate them into English as it would be to translate the terminology of an exact science into Zuñi. I have, however, introduced this approximation to illustrate not only the Indians' powers of observation, but also to give a clear example of the terms by which any given period from planting time to harvesting time may be designated; for the Zuñi, by simply adding a syllable expressive of time to any of the above expressions, thus divide the quarters of the “nameless months.”

## CHAPTER VI

### I'-NO-TE-KWE A-WEN I'-TÂ-WE, OR THE "FOOD OF THE ANCIENTS"

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a person, likely of the Zuñi people, dressed in traditional patterned clothing. They are standing and supporting a long, straight pole or tool horizontally across their shoulders with both hands raised to grip it.</image-desc>

There is a wonderful degree of ingenuity shown in the methods employed by early humans for the production and preparation of food. By primitive man, I mean here the chief figure of a pristine picture faintly lit up against the darkening mists of antiquity by the dim rays of tradition. These rays even now flicker from the hearts of the <term>Zuñi</term> and throw their fading glow backward through, it may be, a thousand generations of men, and westward over desert ranges far toward the slopes that border the "Ocean of the Sunset World."

These were gathered with a sense of fearful awe from the distant sea and shaped with steady persistence using flint tools against blocks of gritty stone. More of the same shells, though smaller and of different shapes, are strung on sinew or hair along with scales, fangs, and glistening stones of magical power to adorn his neck.

Fastened to this in front, or held by a strap around her neck, is a lighter and longer garment of dressed skin that widens toward the bottom. It is wrapped around the thighs and skewered together at the back or side, forming either an apron or a skirt, as you prefer.

Such as these were the remote ancestors of the Zuñis, scattered over a thousand plains instead of just one, slowly working toward a civilization that—having already reached the halfway point—would have ultimately rivaled the Aztecs and Incas in its barbaric splendor and artistic convention, had it not been stunned by the <term>culverin</term> <note>An early form of cannon or long-range field gun</note> of the Spaniards. So too, with only the slightest variation in detail and background, were the progenitors of every civilization on the globe today. Therefore, the story of these particular ancient people—Indians though they may be—who fortunately still dwell within the reach of memory and monuments, is certainly of interest. It may give us a glimpse, by comparison, of how prehistoric man, evolving from a harsh environment, created the possibilities for all that we prize today: food, clothing, and tools, as well as religion, science, and art.

Therefore, pardon me if I briefly record, as an introduction to the cuisine of the modern Zuñi, the first chapter of this prehistoric story.

That the primeval Zuñi was not unlike what tradition has painted him is evidenced by the myths, institutions, and language of his modern lineal descendants, and by the remains he left in the winding trails of his centuries of migration. According to these various sources, he must have been, even in those ancient times, rather superior to the surrounding tribes. Perhaps his closest representative today is the Havasupai, or Coçonino, of Cataract Canyon in Arizona,<sup>22</sup> knowledge of whose daily life serves, I confess, to give color and vividness to some details that would otherwise lack these qualities in the following paragraphs. It thus happens quite naturally that Zuñi tradition will tell you in obscure yet poetic language that the "Seeds of the Ancient were sown only by the Beloved, and his herds herded by the Gods of Prey themselves;" which, interpreted, signifies that he gathered the seeds cultivated by the winds and rains alone, and that his herds—the deer, antelope, and other animals of the hunt—were so wild that none could watch and follow them except the brotherhood of the coyote and the mountain lion.

The story of ancient food can only be half told within the limits of this paper on breadstuff. Half told indeed! For the ancient Zuñi depended on the hunt more than anything else for his survival, especially during winter. During that season, the weather assisted his simple yet effective inventions (snares, stone-tipped weapons, pit-falls, and massive stockades or corrals sometimes covering thousands of acres), making animal food plentiful and reducing the need to deplete his limited stores of roots, fruits, and seeds.

Among the high mountains grew many trees which, stripped of their outer bark and scraped, yielded a crisp pulp and sweet fiber—hard to digest, it is true, but nonetheless welcome to an appetite sated with meat. Most valued for this kind of food and easily accessible with his crude instruments was the yellow pine, thousands of the trunks of which were annually whitened on their southern sides by the scrapers of the ancient Zuñis. Often only the pulp obtained in this way was eaten raw, and the stringy, astringent fiber was wrapped into bundles—huge skeins—and carried home for cooking. Deep down in the sand which bordered, and for a time almost choked, the starved streams flowing from the mountains, the juicy roots of certain rushes were dug. These were sweet and earthy in taste, and although they were scarcely more nutritious than the bark pulp, they were, like the latter, welcome for the variety they provided. They were eaten raw or else slightly toasted in the ashes, dipped in salted water, and used as relishes for roasts of jerked meat. As the season progressed, the rush stems grew tough and the licorice became more bitter than ever; they were replaced with great quantities of watercress (*pi'-k'ai-a*), which is similar in taste and appearance to the celery we all prize, though smaller. It grew abundantly in every spring and living stream, and was boiled and eaten with other food. Each day, the leftovers were made into flat, compact cakes and dried with salt into greenish-black, very stemmy, and hardened bricks, which were packed away for future cooking.

plants furnished food material. Everywhere that rain had fallen on the lower plains, a small variety of milkweed grew in brief and sporadic luxuriance. This plant bore an abundance of little seed pods resembling those of common mustard, although they were a trifle plumper. These were called *thla'-pi-a-we*, meaning “hanging pods.” With their skins removed, they were eaten raw, boiled with other foods, or toasted in hot ashes and soaked in the all-important brine-sauce with mashed onions.

A type of wild, hard-shelled squash—from which the varieties of the true garden plant cultivated by the Zuñis today were undoubtedly derived—grew abundantly in moist arroyos. Its fruit, while still green, was cooked in various ways. Mainly, however, it was boiled into a paste, mixed generously with rancid suet, and fried on hot stone slabs. In this form, it resembled eggplant fried in butter; curiously enough, the strong smell and flavor of the suet were only recognizable in it to a limited extent.

A great luxury was a kind of puff-ball, or

During early summer, the unripe seedy pods of the yucca (Spanish bayonet, or palmita), a quart or two of which may sometimes be gathered from a single stalk or spike, were much sought after by the ancient Zuñis. They were boiled extensively either in water or in water and ashes. When afterward cleaned, they looked much like gherkins, which indeed they prove similar to in taste when pickled in vinegar. They were eaten either plain or with a generous amount of the flavored brine-sauce (*kʻiä′thl-kʻo-se*). Like them, the gummy hearts of a species of the century plant (agave), which had a flavor like cauliflower, were prepared in the same way. Their jealousy and hostility were undoubtedly attributed to the observation that either was equal to the other as food, and both were poisonous if eaten raw.
