> “That is the way the plants of the Beloved scolded one another in the days beyond guessing; but all the same, the *na’-pi-an-we* keep splitting down the belly, and the *su’-pi-an’-we* grow very red at the ends of their noses where the sun strikes them, even to this day.”

With the end of summer—during the middle and latter parts of which rare but abundant rains have fallen—behold the deserts of the Southwest! Weeds, grasses, and shrubs are spread abundantly, though in patches, all over the vast sand plains, competing even more richly with the dark woodlands on the high, wide mesas. In the canyons and down the mountain slopes grow the wild fruit trees and nut-oaks; they possess a fleeting ambition for forest grandeur, yet remain in tangled dwarfishness. The dust-shrouded world has suddenly turned “blue with the mist-laden breaths from Summerland!” or so the Zuñis say of this greenery. Everywhere the “fields of the Beloved” are ripening their harvests. I can no longer, therefore, follow the ancient Zuñi in the order of his gathering.

I have thought it best, therefore, to tell, in the order of their simplicity as food, first how he used the natural fruits and nuts of the forests and valleys, then how he collected and processed the tougher materials and seeds which required the full exercise of his native genius and industrial skill to make them fit food for his palate, however unrefined this may have been judged in the preceding recipes for improvised dishes.

First to ripen, and also the most important among the fruits, was the datila, called *tsu'-pi-a-we* (see plate x, *f*) instead of *su'-pi-a-we*, because of its blushing color when ripe. Few who have not visited the Southwest in autumn imagine that, dry and barren though it may be throughout most of the year, a fruit rivaling the banana in size, shape, color, and extreme sweetness grows there in abundance on the warmer plains. In the course of time, these cylinders grew quite solid and gummy, and became semi-translucent like the gelatin ink rollers used by printers. In taste, the food resembles black licorice. A little slice, being hacked off, was immersed in two or three quarts of water. When it was thoroughly soaked, it was stirred, churned, squeezed, and strained, until a dark-red, pasty fluid was formed. Hardly any delicacy known to the ancient Zuñis ranked more highly than this, or commanded such extravagant bargains in trade with the surrounding tribes.

In the dry season or the wet, there was one class of fruit that rarely failed; therefore, we find modern ceremonies and ancient folklore teeming with allusions to it—the cactus. Of the many varieties of this plant growing in the Southwest, three were especially fruitful, bearing juicy, plump berries with a sour-sweet taste that was particularly pleasant during the hot, dry season in which they ripened. Of these, the *kâ-shi*, or formidable club cactus, bore the largest and perhaps sweetest fruit (*tui'-a-we*), which was a brilliant though dark scarlet color, and in shape and size not unlike an okra pod. The *shu'-ne-po* and *me'-wi* (plate x, g), two varieties of the low-lying chain cactus, bore red and yellow fruit which, though smaller, was more abundant and less spiny, and therefore preferred.

Among the sandy gorges of the upper plains, mesas, and mountains, abundant low bushes grow, bearing very juicy little yellow berries called *k'ia'-po-ti mo'-we*, or the "juice-filled fruitage." These berries were highly favored as food by the ancient Zuni. They were collected in great quantities and boiled or stewed, forming a sweet but tart sauce which, although not quite as acidic, otherwise resembled the cranberry.

Another favorite berry was the small and equally tart fruit of the wild currant, called in Zuni *ke-la shi'-u-ni*, or the "first to leaf out," which grew along the edges of <term>malpais</term> mesas in a lush greenery rarely seen in the Southwest. Like the latter two, the chokecherry or "bitter hanging-fruit" was a frequent ingredient in sauces. The wild plum, or *si'-lu-e-la mo'-we*, was used not only in its raw and stewed state, but was also dried and preserved for later use.

In late autumn, enormous quantities of sweet, tiny acorns were gathered from the dwarf oaks that grew everywhere in the mountains of the Southwest, and even more plentiful stores of the *he'-sho k'u'-we*, or piñon-nuts, which grew in great abundance on the low piñon trees of almost every mesa or mountain plateau. First among them was the *k'u-shu-tsi*, a kind of purslane or portulaca, not unlike the garden pests of the same genus in the East. This plant bore plenty of a small, black, very starchy, and white-kerneled seed. It was gathered by pulling the plants just before the seed had ripened, then drying and threshing them either by shaking or by pounding them over mats or screens. A method of gathering seeds that had progressed too far toward maturity was to sweep up the surface of the ground where they grew—which was usually sandy—dust and all, and afterward to carefully winnow the seeds from the soil.

An equally important seed, though less abundant, was produced by the *suthl'-to-k'ia*, a certain round-topped weed resembling the common pigweed or goosefoot of the East in its grain stalks and foliage, but more bushy; it undoubtedly belongs to the *Chenopodium* genus. once by placing a closely woven, large, shallow tray near each promising bush and energetically slapping the bush with a wicker fan or scoop. With the possible exception of the piñon nut and sunflower seed, this grain is probably the richest and most delicious ever known to either the ancient or modern Zuni, and its decline as a food source must undoubtedly be attributed to the difficulty of producing it rather than to any lack of quality.

Another plant, blue-leafed but otherwise resembling the last one described—though probably not of the same genus—provided seeds which, although less rich and oily, were more valuable if we may trust tradition and their taste. In fact, they were as similar to corn as any of the wild grain varieties used by the primitive Zuni. Therefore, the archaic name by which it was known, *mi'-ta-li-k'o*, means "father-in-law of corn," as nearly as can be determined by its etymology. These seeds were gathered in the same way as those of the *suthl'-to-k'ia*.

supplied to the ancient Zuni. One was the *te'-shu-ko-na* ("that searched for"), or a kind of wild rice, and the other was *pish'-shu-li-a* ("sweep rush"), or a feathery grass. Both of these grew on the wetlands of the Southwest and furnished rich grains. The height to which these plants grew allowed the women to sweep the seeds into large conical panniers (plate x, *b*) without having to remove the baskets from their backs.

Last on this long list, and perhaps the most important as the actual predecessor of the modern bean (although it was very rarely made into bread), was the *no-k'iä-mo-li-a*, or wild pea. It is more accurately a bean than a pea, although it must be admitted that it is shaped like the latter.

These various nuts and seeds were prepared for food in quite similar ways, and several varieties of them were often mixed together to form a single kind of bread or cake. For this reason, I have not discussed them separately, as I did with the bark, root, and fruit products, but have thought it better to create, as it were, a brief chapter on the cooking methods for which they provided the essential ingredients.

These chapters are just as indefinitely separated, then, even though their names are different.

was placed, along with two or three quarts of the seeds or nuts. The operator, quickly squatting, grasped the tray at opposite edges, and with a rapid, spiral motion of the basket, kept the grain and coals dancing separately round and round, yet almost touching one another, meanwhile blowing on the embers with every breath to keep them alive and free from ashes. So dexterously was all this done that the grains were evenly browned, yet none of them scorched; and the delicate basket, protected by the thin coating of clay that had grown hard through long use, was never burned by the fiercest heat of the moving coals. If the seeds were thus made more palatable, less likely to germinate when kept for a long time, and easily processed on the mealing stone, how much more did the later Zuñis owe to this early industry. For with the separation of the thin clay lining from its osier matrix <note>A foundation or mold made of willow branches.</note>—which was baked hard enough in some instances to form a vessel by itself—behold! the potter's art is born.<sup>25</sup> And probably from this crude beginning, by easy yet gradual steps, all the marvelous beauty and per-

<meta>This page continues the argument that the development of Pueblo pottery and weaving was directly derived from basket-making techniques, specifically noting how the physical forms and designs of woven vessels were replicated in clay.</meta>

fection of Pueblo fictile <note>Made of clay or earth; pottery.</note> productions were matured. Did I say most probably? I may now say most certainly; for the spirally built cooking pot of the older Southwestern ruins (pl. xi, *b*) was but the reproduction in clay—rough surface, zigzag ornamentation, and all—of the spirally woven basket-bottle (*a*). The name of this earlier object lingered on to distinguish the "basket in clay" as but the offshoot of the basket in osiers <note>Flexible willow twigs used in basketry.</note>. In no other way can the angular and other extremely conventional features of the ancient Pueblo ceramic decorations be explained than by referring them to the imitation of basketry patterns, which were themselves the mere outgrowth of discolored splint lines. Moreover, by a similar train of reasoning, it is seen that the Pueblos also owed the art and patterns of weaving—embroidery and all—to basketry. Almost positive proof of this exists today in the etymology of the names of stitches and designs.

Does the reader then realize with me how far-reaching the influence of our breadstuff has been?

The portions of the parched seeds and nuts that were required for immediate use were stored in bags around the edges of the lodge. These bags were of various colors or materials to distinguish their contents and were used as seats during the day and as pillows at night. The rest of the grain was carried away to the granaries. These were formed by filling the cracks and plastering the interiors of any suitable holes in the cliffs with mud, specifically those that happened to be protected by overhanging rocks. When filled, these were closed with simple masonry made of such cleverly selected materials that the finished storehouses were almost indistinguishable from the formations around them. Before the mud plaster with which these semi-natural bins were cemented had dried, the owner used his fingertips to stamp into it not only figures indicating the variety of the contents, but sometimes special marks of ownership, or totems; these totems were as faithfully respected as a seal is among ourselves. In this way, the grains were at once stored away and protected from moisture and the damage caused by

For mush, the meal was left coarse and added to boiling water until a thick, sticky mass was formed, which was no longer possible to stir. Whatever was left over of this half-cooked mush was rolled into balls, flattened out and dried, or baked on the embers; no doubt, the earliest suggestion of bread arose from this practice of economy. Bread of other kinds soon followed, as a few selected recipes might well show; but let us first consider some related culinary inventions.

It should be kept in mind that these ancients had to boil foods using hot stones. Two methods deserving of attention undoubtedly survived many attempts to thoroughly cook mush in this way without either filling it with grit or wasting it. Some coarse meal was moistened with enough hot water to make it sticky. This was thoroughly kneaded and rolled into little, elongated balls or cylinders. Griddle cakes were made by cooking a mixture of equal parts of fine and coarse meal with as much scalding water as possible. The resulting paste or batter was poured over hot, well-polished slabs of sandstone.

However, their most perfect oven by far was the smaller of their granaries. These natural cavities, which human skill had only completed as receptacles, were seldom used for baking except when great feasts or long journeys required large quantities of bread. At the end of this time, the "closing stone" was broken down and the loaves were taken out—dark blue or brownish-gray in color, but thoroughly cooked and as palatable as any bread devised since by even the most modern Zuñis.

They affirm that by thus nourishing themselves with however little of the food of their forefathers, they partake of the hardiness, courage, wisdom, and possibly some of the supernatural qualities with which they do not fail to endow their remote ancestors. How long the ancient Zuñis lived, as described here, on the products of nature and the hunt alone, we do not know, nor may we ever know; but of this we may be certain: that the scenes and generations of their life shifted many times during that long period, and that at the same time as their organization into true clans or tribes—or at any rate early in their history as such—they became horticulturists to a certain extent. There is evidence that upon their first arrival in the desert country, they had to displace, or at least to guard against, the raids of a ruder people; hence the remains of their older villages are perched among the most isolated and grim lava mesas, far out of reach, and often near caves or over tremendous fissures. It was during this middle period, as we may call it, that—no longer afraid of any enemy—they divided into small clans or large totemic families, following wherever soil moisture, the presence of water, or other requirements for their limited cultivation led them. Consequently, everywhere within the region claimed by tradition as their habitat at one time or another, we find the broadly scattered ruins of single houses, both small and large.

It is interesting to note the evidence of language in this connection. The Zuñi name for a Navaho lodge, which is a sort of beehive-shaped structure built of sticks and earth, is "*leaf-lodge*" or "*brush-roof*." We may infer from this that the earliest form of hut among the Zuñis was shaped like the Navaho *hogan*, but roofed with leaves, bark, or brush. The modern name for a house is *k'ia'-kwin-ne*, from *k'ia'-we*, water, and *kwin*, the place of, which indicates that the first regular houses were single and distributed according to the occurrence of water in any way. Again, the name of an upper story or room is *osh'-te-nu-thlan*, from *o'shte*, a rock-shelter or shallow cave, and *u'-thla-nai-e*, surrounding or built around. This gives evidence of exactly what the ruins of the scattered houses show: namely, that at the beginning of the peace of the middle period, these houses were one-storied. As time went on and the cultivation which characterized this period was developed, distant, more savage tribes—the Bedouin element of Desert America—tempted by the rich plunder offered by the little isolated farmhouses, descended upon them, driving the inhabitants to seek shelter, not in the lava regions where their all-important corn

Here, on shelves or under shallow grottoes, which everywhere characterize the sandstone canyons of the Southwest, they built the first "cliff-houses" like swallows' nests. The necessity of finding shelter for the whole clan led to the construction of second and even third stories against the rock wall of the cliff. Naturally, this portion of the dwelling took the name most characteristic of it—the portion "built around the cave roof." We only have to suppose that when, in an interval of peace, the cliff fugitives descended to rebuild their farmhouses, the idea of the second story was carried with them, and that its first name, slightly modified, remained, as it has even to this day. Consistent with all this is the evidence furnished by the later house ruins of the middle period, which are sometimes two and even three stories in height.

I have ventured these details because they bear very directly on all that relates to even the daily lives of those whom they concern. The introduction of horticulture, for instance, enabled the Zuñi to build and live permanently, which fostered the cultivation of arts and industries, customs, etc., that were previously limited or unknown. The crude, half-spherical cooking vessels—first made of spirally woven grasses and osiers <note>willow branches used in basketry</note>, then of spirally built ropes of clay—now assumed more regular and ornate forms. Since the necessity of frequent changes of location no longer existed, this pottery was not subjected to the frequent breakage caused by journeys; hence, it gradually replaced the wicker canteens, water bottles, boiling vessels, and roasting trays. may seem, the medieval Zuñi had already advanced far toward his ultimate barbaric status of culture.

Although he continued to gather and prepare wild fruits, nuts, and grains, one added source of supply—*corn*—outweighed them all; for was it not the author of his improvements, the object of his affection, care and devotion, the sure promise of his mastery of the desert?

We may now turn to the foods he made from it. Most easily prepared among these were the green-corn preparations. As with ourselves, the ears were roasted on the coals (or, as he called it, “ripened”), or boiled in his little narrow-necked pots of clay. The delicacy of the year was the far-famed succotash, made by scraping the milky kernels from the ears, mixing them with little round beans, which had now come to be domesticated, and with bits of fresh meat, the whole being seasoned with salt, thickened with sunflower-seeds, <term>suthl’-to-k’ia</term>, or piñon-nut meal, and boiled until reduced to an almost homogeneous stew. common to the Zuñis, still a favorite with their distant, primitive neighbors, the Havasupai—a dish so delicious that no green-corn cooking of civilization can boast anything better—was made by scraping the kernels off in great quantity and grinding them thoroughly in their own milk with sunflower seeds and green squash. Sprinkled with salt, this paste was boiled until evaporation left it thick and gelatinous like curdled milk, although it was more sticky when warm and more solid when cold.

Of course, baked corn—not baked in underground ovens, but in the abandoned granaries of a former period or in the dome ovens (see pl. xiv, xv) nearby—was well known.

After the corn had ripened, two methods of making it edible were extremely simple. While still on the ear, it was toasted, or, if in the kernel, it was parched. This parching was accomplished in several ways. The crudest of all these was burial and constant stirring in hot ashes; but the favorite process was to half-fill a *thle'-mon-ne*, or black, shallow roasting pot or pan (pl. xi, *d*), with clean, dry

<header>ZUÑI BREADSTUFF</header>

sand. The pot was then set over the fire until the sand became thoroughly heated, at which point the corn was poured in and constantly stirred with a bundle of hardwood sprigs (*e*) tied so loosely at the middle that they could be spread apart so that the sand and corn might easily pass between them. When the kernels were well browned and swollen, a careful shaking of the toasting vessel brought all of them to the top, from where they were easily separated from the sand. From the corn parched in this way, a highly concentrated and nutritious substance was made; the grains were first cracked, re-toasted, and then ground into fine flour. A little of this flour stirred into cold water made a gruel that required no cooking and was capable of sustaining life alone during long journeys, where a light load and ease of preparation were essential requirements. Mixed with water and sweetened by the methods described earlier, or luckily by the addition of ground licorice root, fermented and slightly boiled, it made a thin syrup or sweet gruel (*tsa'-shi-we*), which was always the favorite at the Zuñi evening feast.

When the corn was intended to be eaten with no further preparation than parching, salt—if it was abundant enough—was used instead of sand. This gave the kernels roasted in it a delicate seasoning that could not be achieved by the cruder methods described earlier.

As simple as it was for a cereal food, one variety or another of this parched corn formed one of the main staples of the diet, not only for the people described here, but among all the more advanced tribes of ancient America. As proof of this, one does not need to search far into the records of our early explorers and pioneers to find repeated mentions of it. Nor are prehistoric monuments lacking in evidence of its widespread use. Among the forest <term>middens</term> of central New York, in the ashes of excavated mounds along the Mississippi valley, frequently in the granaries, cliff ruins, and caves of the great Southwest, and even in the collections from the <term>huacas</term> of ancient Peru, I have found these toasted grains. Although they are carbonized by age, they remain preserved and unbroken long after the

...which the Zuñis call "The Young Men Who Were Fond of Parched Corn and Sweet Gruel, or The Four Awkward Suitors."

In ancient times, though not very many lifetimes ago, there stood four towns in the valley of the Great Flowing Waters (El Rio Grande del Norte, of eastern New Mexico). One of them was where San Felipe now stands, another was over the mountains to the east where people now gather turquoises, the third was far to the north, and the fourth was toward the south. Who can tell the names of all these towns? I cannot, for they were not the homes of our ancestors. But anyone who looks where they once stood will see their ruins, and many others in between, on the bluffs and in the mountains along the valley of the Great Flowing Waters.

Well, in those days there lived in *We'thlu-ella-kwin* (that was the name of Old San Felipe, you know) an elderly and wealthy <term>cacique</term> who had an only daughter. This maiden was considered the prettiest of her tribe. She was proud, and when she went down to the river in the evening to get

In the northern pueblo at that time lived a young man who was a good hunter and had blankets and shell beads of his own. This young man was very timid and bashful. He neared the cornfields that surrounded Old San Felipe, and a little after dark, he stole into the plaza that fronted the house of the <term>cacique</term>. The house was large, and the old <term>cacique</term> had many relatives, among them many young men—nearly all of whom were married—who were fond of sitting in his house on autumn and winter evenings and smoking as they told stories by the light of the fire, for the old man was merry and hospitable.

Well, the young man looked at the windows of the house. The red light was shining brilliantly through them. “Ha!” he said in his heart, “the house is full of visitors; otherwise, why would the fires burn so brightly? What shall I say when I go in? Oh yes; I will say, ‘My fathers and mothers, my sisters, friends, and brothers, how have you been these many days?’” He kept repeating this to himself, just as a novice repeats prayers before his initiation. Meanwhile, he peered in through the windows. They were very small and high, and he could see only the feet of those sitting inside. “Perhaps I know some of them,” he thought. “If I do, that would make it easier for me to go in.”

Placing one hand on one side and the other on the other, he gently lowered himself until he could see the shins of the visitors. He stretched down a little farther and could now see their knees and the chins of some of the shorter ones. “Only a little farther,” he thought, when suddenly the bundle, giving way, knocked him on the head, his hands slipped, and, poor fellow! down he tumbled, end over end, into the room below. He jumped up—he did not know what to say. Then he remembered his purpose and cried out, “Oh yes; I—I mean, my—my fathers and mothers, my sisters and brothers, how are you after these many days?” Everybody was surprised, but they now began to laugh so hard that the bashful boy, losing heart, fled headlong up the ladder. That was the last they saw of him, for he ran home and never had the courage to try again.

Now, a young man who lived in the pueblo on the Turquoise Mountain happened to hear the cacique’s relatives telling the story of the bashful northern fellow. “Ha-ha, wa-ha!” he laughed with the rest; but he thought, “What a stupid fool! ## CHAPTER IX

### TÂ'-A I'-TÂ-WE, OR THE "FOOD OF THE SEED OF SEEDS"

<image-desc>A historiated initial 'H' depicting two Zuñi women in traditional attire walking in profile, carrying a wooden litter or platform between two vertical poles. The poles and the platform form the shape of the letter 'H'.</image-desc>
Here, we no longer need to follow the methods of the ancient Zuñi bread-maker through the uncertain light of tradition or the barely more satisfactory guidance of comparative study. We can now visit the homes of her modern descendants and observe—if we are willing to accept their hospitality (which is not always easy!)—every step of their process in preparing bread.

First, however, let us consider the changes that gathered the scattered inhabitants of the cliff and valley houses (described in a previous chapter) into pueblos—some of which amazed the Spanish explorers with their organization and size.

<vocab>Zuñi, pueblos, Tâ'-a i'-tâ-we, bread-maker, Spanish explorers, cliff houses, valley houses, tradition</vocab>

<summary>This chapter begins an exploration of modern Zuñi bread-making by observing contemporary practices rather than relying on tradition. It introduces the historical consolidation of scattered cliff and valley dwellers into the large pueblos encountered by Spanish explorers.</summary>
<keywords>Zuñi, bread-making, pueblos, Spanish exploration, cliff dwellings, Tâ'-a i'-tâ-we, cultural transition</keywords>

--- Page 316 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of the Zuñi ancestors, describing how increasing conflict with nomadic groups forced the sedentary "house-builders" into defensive cliff dwellings and shifted their subsistence towards greater agricultural dependency.</meta>

<page-num>290</page-num>
-><header>ZUÑI BREADSTUFF</header><-
-><sig>VIII</sig><-

The raids of predatory bands of savages from the border regions of the desert areas, where the house-builders established their homes and lands, increased along with the prosperity, population, and growth of the house-builders' domain. This also affected the tribes that—having been subjugated by them or encouraged by their example—imitated their industry, until almost all were driven nearly permanently to the cliffs of fertile canyons. Here, regular villages were built instead of single houses wherever a foothold could be found out of the reach of attack (pl. XII). Even if hundreds of the enemy came! These houses—which were essentially suspended midway between earth and air and overlooked the crops—were accessible to the inhabitants via ladders they pulled up after them, but were impossible for a stranger to scale. Now the sunflower, cultivated along with corn, assumed greater importance; tradition says that the cliff-dwellers, who were often besieged from a distance, were barred from the privilege of hunting and were therefore forced to survive for long periods of time on the products of

these older Pueblos, less varied, it is true, and differing in a few of the methods and materials of its composition, was nevertheless so like the latter—indeed, even that of today—that the following descriptions, except where otherwise specified, must be regarded as embracing the cookery of both periods.

The green corn, boiled, roasted, and baked, stewed and fried; the ripe corn, toasted and parched, have already been mentioned; yet there remain one or two other types of food prepared without the use of the mealing-stone, or <term>metate</term>.

Almost as simple as the parched corn was the *mi'-li-a-we*, which was nothing other than baked corn boiled on the ear. A variety of food very like this was called *tchu'-li-a-we*, ordinary corn on the ear being roasted or browned over the coals, then shelled and boiled in water, either with or without meat. A more elaborate food was called "skinned corn," which was similar in many respects to the hulled corn of the Northern states. The corn being first thoroughly

Passing over the various dishes which correspond to our hasty pudding, mushes, and the like, which were all well known, we may be interested to find out how the settled, semi-civilized, pueblo Zuñi improved on the baked things of his farming or cliff-dwelling predecessors. His most notable advance was perhaps the introduction of ashes, or of very finely ground lime, called *a'-lu-we*, mingled with salt into fermented mush-yeast to overcome its acidity. The most prized leaven of his time, however, was chewed *sa'-k'o-we* mixed with moderately fine meal and warm water and placed in little narrow-necked pots over or near the hearth until fermentation took place, when lime flour and a little salt were added. Thus a yeast, in no way inferior to some of our own, was compounded. In addition to its leavening qualities, this yeast had the

The greater variety and refinement of cooking that this yeast made possible for the Zuñi people also required vastly improved culinary methods and appliances. This undoubtedly gave rise to a special room for cooking, which we may, without exaggeration, call the kitchen. I hope to be excused for pausing to describe one of these rooms, using those I am familiar with in modern Zuñi, at least, as my model. Behind the “sitting-place,” as it was called (or the combined dining and living room), entered through a narrow doorway and unlit except for the gray light that struggled down its broad chimney or drifted out from the flicker of its almost constant fires, was the small kitchen of those ancient days. In the dim twilight of this place, the uninitiated would have stumbled at almost every step over its furnishings; for scattered over the floor,

Perhaps belonging to this same class of food, although counted among the delicacies of the Zuñis, was the <term>*ä'-tea-mu-we*</term>, a kind of sweet pudding. It was made of yellow cornmeal, a portion of the batter of which was sweetened either by prior chewing and fermentation or by the addition of dried flowers. This batter was most skillfully wrapped in green corn leaves preserved for the purpose by drying and made flexible as occasion required by immersion in hot water. Perhaps more complex than any of the previously described products of the ancient Zuñi kitchen were the <term>*tchu'-tsi-kwah-na-mu'-we*</term>. These were made by hulling corn, then grinding it with water, precisely as paints are ground by artists with oil. This batter, fine and sticky, well seasoned with lime-yeast, was wrapped in broad husks carefully folded over and tied at the ends, then boiled. The batter was solidified by the boiling and, when done, greatly resembled well-cooked gristle or tough gelatin. Large quantities of these rubber-like dumplings were made at once, as the process of their manufacture was tedious and laborious. When cold, they were reheated by roasting on the embers or by baking in the little hearth-cists of the kitchen.

A crude kind of batter-cake, yet much of an improvement on the variety described before, the forerunner, undoubtedly, of the most important breadstuff known to the

This was boiled until it became adhesive and then pasted or spread over the well-greased, polished baking stone in the corner of the hearth. Differing from these—being raised with yeast before baking, and therefore thicker and circular in shape—were the <term>*k'os-he'-pä-tchi-we*</term>, or salt tortillas. The dough from which these were formed was invariably made of very finely ground white corn, so stiff that balls of it could be flattened out on a smooth stone. These round, thin masses of dough, first indented on one side with the tips of the fingers, were laid with the roughened surface downward on an extremely hot baking stone, while the other surface was similarly indented. They were then constantly turned until thoroughly done and browned. This same dough, without the yeast and thinner like a batter, was used to make “johnny-cakes” or “corn-dodgers,” which were baked on little flat stones that were first well-heated and then placed very near a hot fire.

# SEED OF SEEDS

The simplest forms of true bread were made by placing fine flour in a bowl, into which enough cold water was poured to make a dough, and sufficient lime-yeast to leaven it. This was then kneaded and molded into thick cakes, which were set aside for a short time to rise; afterward, they were cooked on hot coals by turning them frequently, in which form they were called *mui'-ä-ti-we* (fire loaves), or baked while buried deep under hot ashes. In this shape, they were known as *lu-pan-mu'-lo-ko-na*, or ash-bread, which differed as much from the former as if they were made from entirely different materials. It goes without saying that this bread was also frequently baked, especially for feasts, when it took on most extraordinary shapes under the artistic skill of the Zuñi women (see the initial illustration), in the large dome-shaped ovens <note>plates 14, 15</note> or in the small fire-boxes on the rooftops.

Perhaps one of the most curious delicacies—for it was considered such—ever known to the Zuñis, was made not by baking, but by freezing. This was called <term>thlem-mäthl-to-we</term> (“slab-bread”). The plain variety was simply thin mush reduced to a paste by boiling, then placed between two stones which were laid in cold places and left until thoroughly frozen. The unbaked batter of the <term>tchik-k’we’-pa-lo-kia</term>, or “sweet buried-bread,” boiled for an exceptionally long time and then treated in this manner, made what we might call an exceedingly coarse ice cream; it was certainly prized as highly by these ancient people, to say the least, as that delicacy is among ourselves.

Miles to the west of where the eleven towns of the older Zuñis used to stand, there is a beautiful volcanic hill or mountain, sacred in the oral records of this most revered tribe. It is said to be the home of the countless gods and heroes of the *Kâ-kâ*, or the Dance of Worship; for it raises its steep sides and brown, rounded brow, seemingly out of the very depths of the dark Lake of the Dead. Here, many generations ago, came a beautiful Goddess of the Ocean, the “Woman of the White Shells,” younger sister of the Moon. No less kind than the Moon Mother herself, the most lovely of all beings, this goddess was the special patroness of beauty and grace. She loved to count the daughters of men among her disciples, and like Hathor and Isis of the ancient Egyptians, bestowed an attractiveness almost equal to her own upon those into whose

Now, leaning very lightly on her molina <note>The hand-held grinding stone, typically called a mano</note>, and glancing playfully from beneath her waving locks of hair, she talked to the watching maidens, teaching them how to tease their lovers; then, brushing the hair from her eyes, she turned to the metate, and with gentle and swaying yet rapid movements of her arms and body, worked the rubbing stone with her left hand, while with her right she scattered the shining grains under it. Meanwhile, she sang in time with her work the songs that young women have loved to sing ever since, and young men have loved even more to listen to. Perhaps, in explaining why this is, it would be well to describe the potter's art in full; for it is curious enough to have long ago deserved attention; only, it was not until the later cliff-dwellings and mesa villages were built that it reached its highest productivity and perfection.

The clay which served for their wares was seldom taken from the local quarries without prayers and offerings of atonement. Depending on the kind of vessel to be made, it was the subject of careful choice. It was brought from distant sources of supply in the form of dry lumps, which, as needed, were pulverized on the <term>metates</term> <note>stone grinding slabs</note>, and mixed with crushed quartz, sand, or <term>potsherds</term> <note>fragments of broken pottery</note>, then moistened and kneaded until it was in a condition to be easily dented with the tip of the tongue.

...a little underground kiln or else surrounded on the top and sides, above ground, with a dome of turf and greasewood or other light fuel. Just before the summit of this dome was completed, the woman, muttering a short prayer, threw inside a few crumbs or bits of dried bread or dough; this ceremony was called the “Feeding.” The whole mass was then fired, and blankets were held up to block drafts. Within a few minutes, all was aglow with heat. As soon as the turf or wood had been reduced to cinders, the red-hot vessel was removed with a long poker and gently laid on hot ashes hastily drawn to one side of the fire for that purpose. Here, it was thoroughly coated inside and out with the mucilaginous juice of crushed cactus leaves, with <term>piñon</term> gum being liberally applied in addition to the interior. Another dome, this time of coarser fuel, was quickly built, and the vessel was placed inside and fired again. These vessels were rendered so perfectly fireproof and compact that they could be placed empty over a bed of embers, heated almost to redness, and then have cold water dashed into them without causing any breakage or even cracking. I have often seen this done with fear and futile protests, yet I never witnessed an accident as a result. In the same way, though with the addition of a larger proportion of sand, the women make the <term>crucibles</term> with which the native jewelers melt their silver.

In some details, the process of manufacturing water jars, eating bowls, and other vessels was different. It is true they were built up in much the same way and, when nearly dry, scoured smooth with sandstone; however, the clay from which they were made was either a blue variety or a kind of <term>carbonaceous shale</term> or <term>marl</term>. When the wares had been smoothed, they were coated with a thin wash of whatever <term>argillaceous earth</term> was found to produce the desired body color—white, yellow, red, or pink—and highly polished with small, water-worn pebbles. As I have said before, throughout all of these operations involved in the finishing and decorating of these vessels, no laughing, music, whistling, or any other unnecessary noises were allowed, and conversation was carried on in faint whispers or by signs; for it was feared that the "voice" would enter into the vessels, and that when they were fired, it would escape with a loud noise and such violence as to shatter the ware into pieces. So that this should not happen in any event, the <term>voice-spirit</term> in the vessels—especially those designed for water and food—was fed during the firing. <meta>This page continues the explanation of the "exit trail" in Zuñi pottery, detailing the spiritual consequences of closing this line and how it reflects their beliefs about the relationship between food and the vessels that hold it.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>

<sig>VIII</sig>
<meta>footer: INDIAN NOTES</meta>

"exit trail" (*o-na-yäthl kwai'-na*). If these lines were closed, not only would the subtle source of life be prevented from escaping with food or water, but the woman who "knowingly" connected them (that is, with her eyes open) would either be prematurely struck with blindness, or have the coveted source of life within herself forever closed and thus become as barren as the most chaste of maidens. Therefore, whenever it became necessary to paint over these spaces, the decorator turned her eyes away, and the same custom was observed in sealing the opening at the top of any conical vessel, like the native canteen.

A more comprehensive explanation of all this would involve a long discussion more properly the subject of a scientific treatise than of an article on breadstuff, but I have worked enough, I hope, to show the reader that the Zuñi did not consider the nutritional qualities of food and drink entirely due to their bread and water, but to some degree related to the vessels in which they were contained.

From the little I had seen at the quarries, I gathered some of what follows:

I had seen that while some of the old women were busy in the way I have described, applying piñon gum and rubbing crushed cactus leaves over the hot, blackened objects—which proved to be baking stones—others occasionally placed more fuel on the fires and threw into them little green sprigs of cedar. These latter, besides increasing the signal banners of smoke, were supposed to have some powerful effect on the stones.

Off to one side of the little glade where all this was going on, there were two others still working in a kind of quarry. There, stones were lying in all stages of preparation, from freshly mined blocks, roughly chipped into shape, to those awaiting only the firing process by which all must be tempered before use. These stones were composed of a solid, very light gray sandstone. Those that had been fully worked were four inches thick and nearly four feet long by two and a half feet wide. They were not only as even as though planed, but ground to the highest degree of smoothness (short of a polish) by means of various flat, roughly rounded blocks of sandstone. Even the chipped, less uniform edges shared to some extent in this abrasive finish. Having been worked this far, the stones were left, the old woman told me, for an indefinite length of time to cure; and on occasions like the one (fortunately for me) I had intruded upon, they were carried, with great effort, to the vicinity of the fires, there to be thoroughly dried and warmed before being brought into actual contact with the flames and embers.

The usual number of old women making up a party of "stone finishers" is four or eight, rarely more. Four days before the tempering of the stones, they retire to an estufa <note>kiva</note> or private room, there to fast and engage in certain ceremonies, in which crooning traditional chants and repeating rituals play an important part. During these four days they never come forth except at rare intervals and for a very short time (and even then, under the protecting influence of warning head-plumes), so that they may not be touched by the uninitiated. Yet, during the intermissions of their religious observances, they prepare large cakes of piñon gum, carefully wrapping them in strips of cedar-bark, and in other ways make ready for the work at hand. On the morning of the day following the last night of their vigil, they go in single file, led by a specific clan-priest (usually a "Badger," who under no circumstances touches any of them), to the quarry. Before lifting the stones, before even quarrying any of them, they recite long, propitiatory prayers, casting plenty of medicine-meal to the "flesh of the rock." With other but shorter prayers the fire is kindled by the old priest, who uses as his match a stick of hardwood with which he drills vigorously into a piece of dry, soft root, until the friction ignites the dust of its own making, and to the new flames thus generated, offerings of dry food are made. The stones are then brought,

and when warm enough, placed over the fires; being so constantly anointed with the pitch and cactus juice, which they greedily absorb, that they at last seem solid masses of carbonized substance rather than gritty rock. From the beginning to the end of this tempering process, never a word is spoken aloud, nor is the least excitement or lively action indulged in. Sounds uttered would penetrate the grain of the rock and, being expelled by heat or conflicting with the new “being” (function) of the stone, would cause it to split, scale, or shiver with a loud noise. Likewise, the evil influence of excessive passion or hasty action would be communicated to it, with a damaging effect on its future use.

At certain times the stones are temporarily withdrawn and, being coated with grease, are diligently rubbed with hard, smoothly water-worn cobblestones. After several re-burnings and repetitions of this treatment, they take on a fine black luster that practically amounts to a glaze on their upper sides. They are now considered finished, bundled up in old blankets, and

This priest, by the way, although an important official, leading, as we have seen, in certain of the rites, is made, either through good nature or custom, a general assistant. The one I saw had at least that appearance. He was always puttering about—without accomplishing the slightest good—but stepped aside most deferentially when any of the elderly women came near, and wore that irritable look which men so naturally assume when representing the minority at, for instance, a tea-drinking party. From all this I concluded that his role was a survival of ancient days when his protecting presence was a necessity in times of war. Perhaps the bow and quiver which he carried, for no discoverable purpose other than in conformity to a traditional whim, helped me reach this conclusion.

While they are not, in their completed condition, articles of commerce, several in the lot have been made, so to speak, by subscription, and are eventually well paid for. Setting them up in the kitchen fireplace is an event that ranks with our own old "hanging of the crane," though it is a very different ritual in nature.

When everything has been made ready in the household for which one of them was designed, it is solemnly ushered in by one or two of the elderly women who carved and tempered it. They lean the stone, face to the east, against the wall, and "make it acquainted" with selected ears of corn which are placed on either side of it. The stone, or something about it, is then blessed with rituals and abundantly "invested" with prayer-meal and drinking water offered by sprinkling. Finally, it is taken to its bed or "sitting place" in the kitchen (four strongly built columns of mud masonry in the corner of the wide hearth),

laid out, and a fire of splintered cedar built under it. As it gradually heats—so that it would hiss if moistened with the mouth by way of the fingers—a pot of thin paste, composed of hot water and fine flour of all the six varieties of corn, is set to cook, while a bread-bowl is nearly filled with a similar though thicker paste or batter made in cold water, and placed near the left end of the stone.

The latter is now “tried for heat,” as suggested above, and if found right, is scoured with salt, greased, and well rubbed with an old rag. A small bowl of the sticky, well-stewed paste is also set near the left end of the stone (some drops from each dish being dashed into the fire underneath as a sacrifice), and the first baking begins.

The anxiety which attends this trial is by no means trivial when viewed, as it is by the assembled women, in the light of an oracle. One of the “chosen” elders officiates. It would be a sad occasion if this first effort should fail—which it rarely does—for it would signify that the stone was hostile to some of the six kinds of corn-food to be cooked on it later—or they were hostile to it!

Blankets may be purchased, embroideries for the sacred dance paid for, and pottery-making of any quantity and quality hired; however, the inferior *he'-we* baker dooms her family to tough, uneven, poorly cooked shreds and bundles instead of crisp sheets and light rolls. She is herself doomed to the stinging ridicule of her more fortunate sisters and unending envy of their ability. I know what I am talking about, critical reader, for I have quite often despaired and sought the firesides of more distant relatives when the younger of my adopted Zuñi sisters happened to spread paste over the bake-stone of our inner kitchen. If, for example, she uses too large a proportion of the cooked paste, her *he'-we* will be too tough—"too much like chewing gum," some old grouch will say. If, on the other hand, she mixes in an excessive quantity of the cold batter, it will be "brittle as thin ice," or "like sand, chilling the bones of him who eats it." If, despite all this, she succeeds, what a blessed day it is for her! No matter how poor she may be, she is universally in demand. At the houses of the wealthy on the eve of great feasts; at the clan house-buildings, where more than one vigorous fellow, mindful of his future, is enticed by her presence to the detested work; at all these and many other places—petted, pampered, and lavishly dressed—

she may be unfailingly seen. Like her hardworking, rather more common sister of the milling-trough, she is a flirt. Like her, too, she is a devotee of that wicked, fabled Goddess of the White Shells—at least, so goes the story. But never mind the story! Goddess or no goddess, it is just the same with every tribe on earth.

Six varieties of the *he'-we* are in common use: the yellow, the blue or green, the red, the white, the multi-colored or all-color, and the black. They are the bread of the Zuñis. No meal, however sumptuous, is ever eaten without one or another of them. Most of the colors result from the hues of the corn grains used. If, for instance, yellow *he'-we* is desired, yellow corn exclusively is used for its manufacture. The blue is deepened by the addition of lime-yeast to the meal of blue corn. Green is produced by an equal mixture of blue and yellow meal, and the addition of lime-yeast and ashes. It and the blue are the most constantly used of all varieties. White is made whiter with a little kaolin; black, or rather a dark purple, with certain

charred and powdered leaves. The multi-colored *he'-we* is more difficult to produce. Six dishes of paste are provided, each prepared as if for one of the colors named above. Three of these are cooked (those containing lime or ashes), while the others are left cold. For each sheet of the *he'-we*, a tiny dip into first one and then another of the dishes is made, and each dip is dashed upon the stone. A mottled or brindled sheet is the result. Because its appearance is so much better than its actual eating quality—which is almost its only recommendation—it is rather unpopular except on certain occasions.

Of each variety of *he'-we* except the last one described, several kinds or grades are made. The thick *he-yä'-ho-ni*, usually eaten warm, is formed of several layers; that is, three or four applications are made across the entire surface of the stone before the sheet is removed. It is then turned, quickly replaced, and neatly folded while still relatively moist.

of the Zuñis. Salt and lime-yeast are added to the pastes, and a generous quantity of suet, also salted, is rubbed over the stone before baking. When not intended for immediate consumption, this salty *he'-we* is rolled into neat little sticks or cylinders corresponding in length to the width of the stone. No bread is lighter or more tempting than these *he'-po-lo-lo-we* piled one above the other on the bright wicker trays in which they are served. Another very pleasing kind of wafer bread is the *kwi'-k'ia-he'-we*, or milk *he'we*. In the mixture of the pastes from which this is formed, milk instead of water is used, resulting in a food richer to the palate than "cream biscuits."

The wafer bread that is intended for daily use is baked at once in great quantities. The piles of sheets laid one above another are often so high that they look like huge bales of fine wrapping paper. Partially doubled or folded into masses, which we may call quires, or even reams, they are packed away in permanent half-buried jars provided with close-fitting lids.

## VIII

Thus, the moisture is preserved, which keeps the *he'-we* from crumbling in the fingers as it is eaten, and gives it the peculiar feel and flavor in the mouth that distinguishes it as the most perfect of all known corn foods. Despite the care used in storing it, if this thin food is kept beyond a certain time, it will become dry and far more flaky than the most delicate pastries. The flakes are carefully preserved, together with the crumbs from feasts and the residue from the bread trays of each meal. When a sufficient quantity has accumulated, it is dried further by exposure to heat, then quite finely pulverized by hand. One of the several dishes made from these *he'-we* chips is wafer toast (*he'-la-kwi-we*). The chips, along with salt and unrendered suet or scraps, are thrown into a *thle-mon*, or earthen toasting pan, and stirred until well browned. This, ground on the metate to the consistency of coarse meal, forms one of the staple foods for long journeys. Chief among these latter preparations, however, is the same meal of toasted *he'-we* chips, ground finer and partially cooked

as is the plain cornmeal batter, in another part stirred into cold water and baked a second time on the stone. In this state, it is called double-done *he'-we*. It no longer tastes like the food from which it is remade, but rather like the most delicate pie crust.

A sweet *he'-we* (*he'-tchi-kwa*), bright red in color and resembling "London sugar wafers" in taste, is made from the fine meal of red corn. The cooked portion of the ingredient paste is thoroughly boiled in a decoction of red corn leaves and shoots (plucked earlier in the season and carefully dried for this express purpose). This imparts the color and taste that distinguish it from all other kinds of *he'-we* described so far. Yet another *he'-tchi-kwa* is made by the chewing and fermenting process so often mentioned on previous pages. While neither very sweet nor bright-colored, this bread possesses a peculiar flavor that is highly regarded by the natives, making it extremely popular on the mornings of feast days. bread, or broad *he'-we* (*he'-k'ia-pa he'-pa-lo-k'ia*). Several smooth, thin baking-stones are heated and placed within easy reach. Meanwhile, the paste is thickly applied to the regular *he'-we* stone; each sheet is taken off as soon as it is cooked enough to hold together and is then placed between a pair of the hot baking-slabs. In this way, a pile of alternating stones and thick *he'-we* sheets is built up to a height of a foot or two and allowed to stand until the steam, which at first pours out in great volumes, begins to disappear. The well-baked and pressed cakes (if we may call them such) that result from this are quite brittle, although they are by no means tough when eaten while fresh. Over time, however, they become very hard and—along with the dried pieces of ordinary buried-bread—are reduced to a fine flour for the use of traveling or hunting parties.

Sometimes sweet cornmeal is treated in this or other ways, making a most delicious flour, of which a very little goes a long way toward satisfying hunger. Of all substances known to the Zuñis,

It is then dried for a day or two and thoroughly toasted in the parching pot, ground into coarse <term>samp</term>, toasted again, ground into very fine flour, toasted once more, and then carefully sifted. Processed in this way—accounting for waste and extensive reduction—a bushel of corn yields only a few quarts of flour. A single teaspoon of this powder, when stirred into a pint of water, will make a fairly thick batter; in this state it is drunk, and a few sips are enough to satisfy the most hungry appetite. When combined with meat-meal, or jerked venison that has been toasted and ground up with red pepper and salt, it contains all the elements necessary for human sustenance. # CHAPTER XI

## Khia' I'-tâ-we, or Wheat Food

### THE INTRODUCTION, CULTIVATION, AND USE OF WHEAT AMONG THE ZUÑIS

From where and how did the wheat come, with which the first fields of that golden grain were sown in the desert valleys of Zuñi? Long indeed would be the twofold answer to this double question—so long, that I venture to give only a meager outline of the romantic history which it involves.

Three hundred and fifty-five years ago, a Spanish nobleman and president of New Spain named Nuño de Guzman lived and ruled in a province of Mexico with high-handed extravagance—and with an iron hand as well. Among his many Indian slaves was one named Tejos, who had been captured from the valley of Oxitipar. This

These cities he had visited in the company of his father, who, being a merchant, was accustomed to go there to trade the brilliant feathers of Mexican birds for turquoises and golden treasures, which he said the natives of that country possessed in unlimited measure. Inflamed by the memory of the brilliant conquest of the Aztecs, accomplished only a decade earlier, and anxious, moreover, to rival his political enemy, the great Cortés, Nuño de Guzman set out for the Seven Cities with an army of about a hundred Spaniards and more than 2,000 Indians. Having arrived among the mountains of northern Mexico, he was met by unexpected hardships, and tribes of fierce savages attacked his starving ranks daily, until he was compelled to turn back. Continually hearing glorious reports of Cibola, and always being venerated as a supernatural being while being entertained and assisted on his way by the Indians, he traveled through a desert and into a well-inhabited valley, finely cultivated and filled with large towns. Twisting this way and that through a mountain-encircled plain, and rushing at last into the narrow gateway of a perpendicular wall of strangely eroded red-sandstone strata, it disappears under a dense bed of rushes and cane-grass.

When sought again half a mile below, nothing remains to remind you of it but a feeble brook, lazily sliding past the base of the worn, ancient town of <term>Tâi'-ya</term>, or “Place of Planting.” Up among these rushes, one may soon discover why the life of the stream has departed. Each of these square enclosures is ten by twelve feet, rarely larger. Fifteen or twenty of them make up the plot of a poor man; those belonging to the wealthy, who can afford feasts for many laborers, are several times larger. The soil within them is like that of a garden, and the wheat is planted in rows, arranged crosswise so that it may be easily watered and hoed in mid-summer. The cultivated area extends a mile and a half up and down the valley and is nearly as wide as it is long. Within it, forty families raise their wheat for the winter. use more than his proper allowance of water. As summer wanes and the wheat, grown tall and heavy with grain under so much kind treatment, begins to ripen, the villagers, who mostly departed several weeks ago, return in full force. The harvesting is accomplished by means of knives and short, crude sickles. If a man is fortunate enough to get hold of an American sickle, he immediately breaks off half of the blade and makes two out of it. The wheat is cut off near the head. Huge blanket-bags full of the ears are transported to one of the village's several threshing floors. These are simply cleared circular spaces on <term>argillaceous</term> soil, well beaten down, sprinkled, beaten again until level, and baked in the sun until as hard as brick. There is usually a post in the center; more rarely an arching palisade. The wheat ears are spread fairly evenly over the extent of one of these floors, and a motley crowd of children, horses, and donkeys is let in upon it. The horses go in against their will; the burros for business—part of which is eating (though it is unauthorized); the children go to

A baby, eloquent with the mystery and hunger of the occasion, is tightly wrapped to her back in a blanket; from its ample folds, the baby's muffled cries only faintly emerge. Clinging behind are the little boy and girl, bearing, with compressed lips and heroic half-gasps, the pain of their uncomfortable seat—for they are "the little man and woman of the family," you know! In her left hand this lady carries an old parasol; in her right, a well-sharpened hardwood prod with which she sharply touches a sore spot on the burro's right shoulder. Her feet are tied into the straps of the saddle—the stirrups being too long—and with her heavy, buckskin-wrapped legs (which appear short and indeed are so), she fearlessly thumps the sides of the burro until he groans and staggers, yet he patiently keeps his usual pace. Next comes the old man! His burro is loaded with household belongings. Among these is a cat, sewn up skin-tight in a cotton bag, with its head protrud-

The old man, still jogging along, catches his breath, having struck the animal with all his strength. The <term>burro</term> takes advantage of this lull, which soon rouses the old man again. "So-ho!" he exclaims, "*You* cause of deep thought!"

Whack—"You slave of sticks"—whack—"You anger of the gods"—bang—"Insect—long-eared turtle—take *that*!"—whack-after-whack—"and that." Bang. The last blow, hitting the hock <note>the gambol joint</note> of the male donkey <note>the jack</note>, causes him to twist off the trail with his hind feet and move sideways. "Here now!" shouts his tormentor, as he skips around—quite nimbly for his age—toward the head of the beast, "Get in there, you one-eyed, slow-moving breeder of vermin; get in, I say!"—and cuff-after-cuff the stick goes down on the long, flopping ears of the donkey. And so things continue until the end of the twenty-five miles.

The story is told of one old man who, while administering well-deserved <note>condign</note> punishment to his <term>burro</term>, missed his aim and knocked out the brains of his favorite eagle. He then and there finished the whole business. In his excitement, he killed the cat, broke a couple of water jars, and ended up by killing the donkey.

# WHEAT FOOD

edge, pressing it in turn down the center as she draws the first hand out; and so on alternately (fig. 7), until it all becomes perfectly homogeneous and cohesive. Taking out a little lump of this dough, she wets it, sprinkles it with flour, kneads it on the bread-stone over and over again, rolls it up into a ball, pats it out flat, turns it over upon itself, greases it well all over, lays it on the white cloth, and pricks it full of holes with a grass straw. In this way, the ordinary Zuñi loaf is formed. On grand occasions (such as those described in the concluding chapter), these shapes are fancifully varied. You may see figures of men and women, deer, antelopes, and rabbits, birds, butterflies, sunflowers, and perforated rosettes, quite artistically modeled, although they are rather inclined to lose their detail as they swell while rising. The dough loaves are laid on flat stones or boards and taken to the oven, which has been cleared meanwhile of its fire, swept out and scented with cedar leaves, and placed inside using a long-handled shovel of pine, which is usually quite handsomely carved (pl. xi, *f*). ZUÑI BREADSTUFF

INDIAN NOTES

The oven is full, the vent-hole at the top is plugged, the doorway closed with a heavy stone and plastered, and the bread left baking for twenty minutes to half an hour, or under certain circumstances a longer time. Then the stone is taken down and the loaves are shoveled out. They are crisp, brown, and very light, having almost doubled in size during the baking. The bread is hearty and nutritious, although inclined to be slightly sour if overleavened.

Some of the dough used for bread-making is always reserved and made up into flat cakes like those of corn flour described in an earlier chapter as *he'-pa-tchi-we*, or tortillas. By the addition of milk and shortening, a sort of unsweetened cake, very pleasant and rich, is made in the same way.

### CHAPTER XII

#### HU'-MU-A K'IA-NA-KWE, OR "THE CROONER BANDS"

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap 'Q' where the tail of the letter is an illustration of a drumstick. The word "Drumstick" is printed in small letters near the head of the drumstick.</image-desc>
While I was quietly engaged one winter's day in my little room in Zuñi, I suddenly heard the thrum-thrum and clang-clang of a great drum and many rattles and bells. Old Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa and I were together as usual.

"What is that?" I asked, rising and picking up my notebook and pencil.

"Be dignified, you crazy man; put down that paper-fold and mind your own business; it is nothing but a lot of *hu'-mu-a k'ia-na-kwe*."

"Who are they? Dancers?" I asked.

"Crooners, I said, crooners! Do you hear?"

"What are 'crooners' then?"

"A group of young fools—grown-up boys and girls who get together to work,

# CROONER BANDS

make a lot of noise and little else. Now be dignified!”

The next remark I made, after waiting duly and patiently, produced nothing more than “Shut up!”

So I despaired of gaining any further enlightenment. All day long, the distant *boom-boom* sounded and continued far into the night; but the old man, gloating over my restraint, kept his eye on me. With one excuse or another, he cleverly intercepted any attempt I made to sneak away.

Many days passed, and one chilly morning, well before sunrise, the old fellow burst into my room. He threw a lot of wood onto the fire with as much noise as possible and began to sing at the top of his voice. He picked up a cudgel <note>a short, thick stick used as a club</note> and beat it against the edges of my bedding until I winced, fearing he might miss, and then he snarled out:

“What in the name of idiocy do you want?” for I was terribly sleepy.

“You!” he said. “Get up quickly—something is coming—hurry!” he added, prodding me with the stick quite roughly. “Hurry, or you will be too late!”

“...cuddle, like the American you are, until the drum made you dream of thunder, if I didn’t stir your pulse a little, for I am your elder brother, you know.”

By this time the house was filling with activity. The brother-in-law—we called him “Greasy” sometimes, when he wasn’t there—was straining away at a buffalo hide which he had tied to an enormous drum jar, until his temper seemed, as the Governor said, like an inflammation, and his eyes like bubbles. Others were bringing in corn and wheat, which the old women, who were now beginning to assemble, immediately set about shelling and toasting. The <term>metates</term> were thoroughly cleaned, everything was prepared, all the best blankets in the house were impressively displayed on the poles, and two or three sheep were butchered and thrown into boiling pots barely smaller than the drum. The women of our house went away and reappeared dressed in their best. Soon a young girl entered, then another, and another, until sixteen or eighteen were chattering and laughing together as they laid aside their blue-black shawls and loosened their

“Their villages are very neat. The houses are very well arranged and very tidy. One room is designed for the kitchen and another to grind the grain in; this last is separate and contains a furnace and three stones fixed in masonry. This predicament has given rise to many a story. The most complete of these I ever heard was told to my little Indian nephews and nieces on a very stormy night, not long after the crooning I described above. If I had only known then that there would be a millstone for all my breadstuff, I would have listened more attentively to the tale. ## CHAPTER XIII

### THE STORY OF THE YOUNG HUNTER

VERY long, long ago there lived in the Town of the Winds a big young oaf, as ravenous as a buzzard and as slow to understand as a horned toad. What a fool that young man was, to be sure! Why, he didn't know a pumpkin from a melon; certainly not when it came to eating, for he would cram one down quite as greedily as the other. His father and mother had died when he was a mere infant, so that he nearly starved until teething time, which perhaps was what made him always so hungry afterward. Then his uncle had been killed in war, and so there he lived all alone with his grumbling old grandmother. Now, this young man was strong, like most people of his kind, you know, for all through his growing years he had been storing it

# CHAPTER XV

## HOW HE WAS DIVORCED

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap "A" featuring the letter inside a square frame embellished with ornate floral and vine motifs against a dark, textured background.</image-desc>

ALMOST at the dawn of the next morning, the runners, returning with their burdens, were seen in the distance. In the days when the herds of our ancestors were only wild deer and their kin, meat was more precious than it is now. So it happened that the story of the youth’s success, told overnight, kept the hearths glowing until daylight, and on the rooftops at sunrise the people watched the arrival of the deer-bearers as thirsty travelers watch flying rain-clouds.

“Down in his grandmother’s house, the young man had stirred himself early and was still busy with his plumes and prayer-wands when a messenger appeared at the sky-hole <note>The hatchway or opening in the roof of a pueblo dwelling that serves as an entrance and smoke hole.</note> and summoned him to the rooftop. He was the one who had watched the youth that night when the maiden had also watched him! But the people did not notice his absence, for the warrior-priests had already finished the division and now began to distribute the meat; the shouting was loud and the laughing long as each person received their portion. When nothing but the skins remained—except for the shares of the elders and the youth’s old grandmother—the runners came forward and breathed on the hand of the youth, thanking him for his day of favor, and the people followed, treating him like a father of the tribe.

For a few moments the girl stood by, then she said again:

"My hunter never had a sister, did he?" Still the youth worked the scraper. "Did he?" the girl repeated.

"No," replied the youth, beginning to think of what his old friend, the Coyote-being, had said about this girl, and wondering how it would all come about, and somehow wishing it would. The girl did not let him wonder long.

# CHAPTER XVI

## HOW HE TWICE RETURNED

<image-desc>A rectangular illustration showing a large hand reaching through a doorway to hold a mouse by its tail. The word "DIVORCED!" is printed vertically alongside the left doorframe.</image-desc>

For only a little while did the Mouse-charmed young hunter, or Were-mouse (as we shall call him from now on), bemoan his fate unnoticed. It happened very soon that some field mice went scampering by. A trim little dun-skin happening to lag behind, overheard him; for, although his heart was human, his lament, being voiced through a mouse's muzzle, was made in mouse language.

" 'Ssh tchu!' whistled the little Mouse-woman to her mate, maiden sister, and cross old uncle, 'Who can that be talking?' Up they all sat on their haunches to listen.

The one in front came quickly forward, but stopped. The Were-mouse was so much larger than himself that he stood there quite a while wagging his whiskers and staring as if trying to decide whether to speak or run. Presently he ventured:

"'Friend,' said he, lifting his paw as a sign of greeting, 'we heard you and came to speak to you; but you must come with us or get under some shadows at once. This is a bad place, and it is a wonder you have not been snapped up by a Hooter <note>Likely an owl</note> long ago.'"

"Ah friend, what can I do; where shall I go? I am a man, not a mouse, as you see me," said the Were-mouse, surprised that the little creature could talk to him. "Maybe he is a man like myself, changed into a mouse," he thought. "Ah, now I see! You are like me, a man in mouse form. Oh, tell me how we can get back to Pi'-na—"

"Crazy; I say, crazy," wheezed the broken-nosed old mouse, coming up just then. "What did I tell you? When a mouse turns around inside himself he thinks—"

"Shut up!" exclaimed the Mouse-mate, patting the sand and twitching his bristles. "Let me *talk* to him, will you?"

"*Muh'-hu-tu*," sounded the hoot of an owl somewhere above them. Away the mice scattered, and the poor Were-mouse, too weak and stiff with cold to follow, crawled under a stone, and none too soon either.

Pretty soon, all the mice who had been running about the field seeking fresh spring roots ran in too. So, of course (feeling safe down there), they began to talk, and the young <term>Mouse-mate</term>, who had found the poor <term>Were-mouse</term>, told all about what he had seen and heard. Their leader—a wise, very big old mouse who had seen many hard winters and had even been caught by a wildcat (of which he still showed the marks)—said that he knew there were beings among the <term>High-walkers</term> <note>Humans</note> of creation who, having great power, treated their fellows badly and sometimes toyed with their lives and shapes. He had no doubt this was a case of that kind (he had known such cases), but they invariably died of starvation. He called a council and sent some stout young warriors off with the <term>Mouse-woman</term>’s mate to bring in the “<term>High-walker</term> Mouse,” as he called him. The poor <term>Were-mouse</term> was just trying to crawl out when the warrior-mice found him.

This was the house of the Great Horned-toad Medicine Band. Inside sat a number of very bag-bellied, solemn, old Horned Toads, almost as large as men.

“You have come,” said the master-priest of the Toads, blinking his eyes and limping out to place a seat for the Coyote.

“Yes; may you be happy these days!”

“May you be the same,” they replied. “What would you like, brother, and what do you say?”

### STORY OF THE THREE HORNED TOADS

“‘There,’ he cried, setting his burden down, ‘I have brought my prey; but it is for you to say whether it shall be prey or not.’

“He dropped the Mouse into the hole.

“The three Horned Toad Priests were sitting around a great stone hearth on which a bright fire of sagebrush was burning. When the Were-mouse fell down among them, they did not look up or stop smoking for a long time.

“At last, one of them took his pipe from his mouth and puffed a long cloud of smoke over the Mouse, while the others reached for their rattles and began a low, humming song.

“‘Why have you come?’ asked the Priest.

“‘I was brought,’ said the Mouse.

“‘I know that,’ replied the Priest, ‘but why were you brought?’

“‘Because I became a Mouse,’ the hunter replied, and he told his story.

“‘It is well,’ said the Priest. ‘Sit down and eat.’ He pointed to a small, broken bowl. ‘Drink and eat,’ he said.

“But the Mouse saw only a few drops of water in the bowl and a few crumbs of bread crust.

“‘Eat,’ the Priest commanded. ‘There is enough.’

“And no matter how much the Mouse ate and drank, the bowl remained as full as ever. <note>38</note>”

### VIII

Hardly waiting to ask, he rushed down the ladder and laid the Were-mouse hunter on the floor in front of the sleepy old Toads. The Horned Toads blinked and gaped, but they soon began to rush about as if they had *never* slept. One laid the Mouse before the altar fire, another ran and brought a magic crystal, and blowing the fire into a glow, heated the crystal to redness in the embers. Then the master-priest and his two warriors spread a sacred *mi'-ha* (a ceremonial cotton blanket) over the Were-mouse, caught up their medicine-plumes, dipped them in the terraced bowl of magic water that stood nearby, and sprinkled the shrouded form. Then their incantation and dance began. Every time the song-line was finished and the *shithl'-na* <note>a cabalistic or mystical word</note> was spoken, the figure under the blanket started, growing and growing as the song and dance went on, until the mouse-charmed hunter was as large and as long as a man (pl. xxiv).

## CHAPTER XVII

### ABOUT SOME INDIAN MEALS

<image-desc>A line-art illustration shows the top portion of a southwestern adobe-style building. A wooden pole ladder is propped against the side, and strings of chili peppers are hanging from the edge of the roof. Below the drawing, the caption reads "Drying peppers".</image-desc>

We have reviewed, step by step, the history of Zuñi breadstuff and, in part, the story of the people who made it. We have seen, through the lens of the language, myths, folktales, and flickering traditions of their descendants, how a people many centuries ago were driven by the relentless hand of savage warfare into the forbidding desert regions of the Southwest. We have seen how there, wandering from one scant watering place to another, they gathered the seeds of wild grasses and shrubs, the roots and stems of succulent plants, the bark and nuts of trees, and the fruit of cacti and bushes from which to make their meager breadstuff. How thus always

How, as a consequence of this and the necessity resulting from both their agricultural state and the encroachments of their ever-vigilant enemies, they came to owe to the environment into which they had been so cruelly forced the adoption of their sedentary mode of life, the development of their strange architecture, curious arts and industries, and their remarkable <term>cultus</term> and religion. Meals, and the manner of eating them, are not only the measures of a man’s social standing in Zuñi, but also the indicators of his character and the strange tokens by which the status of little-known tribes and nations are judged. I have often heard characterizations based upon this method of interpretation. I will leave the reader to make his own estimate of their correctness from a number of examples:

> “The Americans eat food with fingers and knives of metal, and talk much while eating,” said an old priest one day; and the response was, “It must be a land of plenty where people refuse to gather morsels with their fingers and are such good tasters that they fear to touch food with their hands! The crows must eat well and the coyotes grow big-bellied in that land. I wish I were a crow or a coyote!”

Of a man who eats with an absent-minded air, opening and closing his mouth in a routine, monotonous sort of way, they will say, “He eats his food as a fish does water!” the obvious inference being that he has plenty of it, and therefore gives it no thought.

If a man seems to enjoy everything placed before him, eating good and bad with equal satisfaction, they will remark, “When the grass dries up and the sheep starve, happy is he! Fat meat and lean, it is all the same!” Or, in a still more pointed allusion: “Why should he want sheep? *Burro*-meat costs nothing!”

When General Beale (then a lieutenant in the United States Army) was exploring the great overland route to California many years ago, he camped at Zuñi. There was a young boy belonging to the Coyote clan of the tribe who either begged or stole so much sugar and hardtack from the soldiers that it nearly killed him. The title of “Ti-ne-ente Meal” (Lieutenant Beale), which he carried ever after (?), served as a constant reminder of this early episode.

One of my adopted sisters in Zuñi was so frugal that she always reheated the boiled meat—sometimes, if economy required it, twice or three times.
