I could continue listing proverbs, witty sayings, and short nicknames related to meals indefinitely; however, enough has already been shared to demonstrate the importance of breadstuff as a measure or standard of comparison in Zuñi, and to introduce the tribe's hospitality.

If this hospitality were more widely known, it would become legendary. Among the neighboring tribes, it already is. The Navahos, for example, were until recently the oldest and worst enemies of the Zuñi (and their mutual hatred has by no means ended). Yet, if one simply pokes his disheveled head inside any window or doorway in Zuñi, the immediate greeting—and often the only one—will be:

->“Enter; sit and eat!”<-

# INDIAN MEALS
VIII

of another native characteristic so at odds with the first that a return to the latter topic will be essential soon, to reconcile us to the belief that both may belong at the same time to a single people.

The stinginess of the Zuñis, to put it mildly, is quite as famous as their generous hospitality. In trade it is, like most main things of their daily life, a matter of religion. The hostess of a lavish meal, where *he'-we* has been piled before the guests as high as their knees, and the major part of a sheep has been boiled into a uniform stew for their delight, will gather from the floor (thriftily swept with a view to this process beforehand) every flake and crumb of the feast, and critically examine each bone that has been dropped, to see if perhaps it may be cracked for the marrow. Any man, woman, or child of the tribe is as welcome as frogs are to water to a place at the family table; but let an unlucky soul find his corn-bin low or his pepper-string empty, and he will have to pay doubly and dearly in service or goods for each grain of corn or red pod!

While any tribal member is welcome to share a family meal, purchasing basic supplies like corn or peppers from another requires heavy payment in labor or goods.</summary>

I am aware that I shall be accused of having romanced in telling this almost incredible anecdote, but those who are familiar with Indians and their ever-changing tribal relations will not find it hard to believe that I erred only in greatly condensing the conversation above. It can be easily understood how Zuñis and Navahos, who have murdered into one another's families during war times, may “forgive” one another with the return of peace. They do it as a matter of policy, knowing full well the unstable quality of their intertribal relations. heartily despises and abhors these inoffensive representatives of a priesthood who persecuted the gods of his forefathers, so much so that any white man who even resembles one of them will meet with only a slow welcome in the town of Zuñi. The Zuñis would as soon think of drinking poison as of permitting a man, woman, or child of that detested race to witness one of their festivals or sacred dances. If a "Don" or "Greaser" <note>A derogatory historical term for a Mexican person.</note> happens to appear while any of the tribal ceremonies are going on, he is met by watchful sub-chiefs and amicably but firmly escorted to a part of the town that is most remote from the scene of celebration, and then locked up. He may rave and swear and call down the vengeance of "El Gobierno" <note>The Government.</note> on the Indians for detaining him, but so long as that festivity lasts, whether it is one day or four, he will be held a strict prisoner. Yet the customs of hospitality are so strict that the unhappy captive is supplied with every delicacy the Zuñi cuisine can produce, his horses or donkeys are fed and watered, and nothing which a favored guest might expect is left undone.

The first English phrase I heard at Zuñi was, “*How li loo?*” (How do you do?), and the second, spoken in an immediate and futile attempt to pull more of my language from a quickly failing store of knowledge, was, “*Cally walamelons?*” (Spanish and English for “Do you like watermelons?”). When I refused—being eager to witness a dance that was going on—the person I was talking to agreed by nodding his head and repeating emphatically, “’At’s good, ’at’s good,” which I strained to interpret as meaning, “As you wish,” though it might have meant that the watermelons were good.

Toward one another the Zuñis, as has already been suggested, practice these rituals even more diligently. A Zuñi might not be on speaking terms with another person, and might even go so far as to refuse to eat with him; but if by any chance that other person should happen to enter his home, he will certainly have a bread-tray placed before him and be told, in a matter-of-fact way, to eat.

I always took the opposite course and usually had the satisfaction of finishing with ease and reasonable comfort, while it cost my neighbor a frightening effort of absorption, a significant amount of time, and many changes of position, leaving him—the victor—with bulging eyes, short of breath, and sitting rigidly upright.

Driven by both their liking for American food and their sense of duty toward a class of hosts they held in deep respect, five of the six Indians I brought East in the spring of 1882 literally suffered untold miseries; for they rarely complained, except to sadly belittle their own abilities.

“Would you have me bring shame upon my nation?” another asked indignantly, as he reached out his hand for a lemon that a generous man on a Chicago, Burlington, and Quincy railroad train offered him.

“Even though we are carried in this swift wagon as if on the wings of the wind!” he continued, taking and waving the lemon. “Is it not a house with many guests?”

He was in the beginning of his hundredth year and had never, during his long life, tasted even a spoonful of acid, except for the slight hint of it that might be found in a green peach or resulting from the fermentation of a meat stew. So I protested, but in vain. He quickly pulled out his hunting knife and cut the lemon in two.

In addition to the accomplishments discussed above, there are others more easily achieved, though just as essential in the line of polite duty toward one's hostess in Zuñi.

To ensure her perfect contentment—that is, on informal occasions—you must smack your lips over her meat stews, linger lovingly and by no means noiselessly over the marrowbones, sip the soup and *tsa'-shi-we* with long, audible gulps, and, if possible, belch vigorously. Indeed, you are quite excusable if you add other less decorous demonstrations as a sort of after-dinner accomplishment. If, for instance, while sitting around when the meal is over—which is, by the way, perfectly proper in Zuñi—you happen to be seized with a mild fit of indigestion, which pleasantly exaggerates all the symptoms mentioned above, you will score a decided success. Your behavior will then be so natural and spontaneous that the happy matron will not fail to attribute it to the strength of her food. Even some slight discomfort on your part will, under these circumstances, be acceptable and flattering evidence that

Aside from these general principles of Zuñi breadstuff etiquette, there are lesser yet equally well-defined duties affecting the relationship of host and guest. The matron of a household is scrupulously clean about her cookery, so far as her intentions go. She will wash a piece of meat like a rag in cold water or the river before putting it on to boil, until every trace of blood and a large portion of the juice is gone; but then, she thinks nothing of laying it on the skin-side of an overturned bed-pelt to drain while she gives the final polish to the inside of the cooking pot with a scrap of old clothing! So, she will move unconsciously from inspecting or combing the hair of one of her beloved children, or picking wool, with no more than a dry brush of her hands, directly to the toasting of tortillas or the mixing of mush. Yet she would resent the liberty hotly if one of her guests happened,

A rather relevant illustration of this may be drawn from my own earliest experience with it.

I was trying hard to win my way into the elusive affections of the Zuñis and took up doctoring. Among my patients was a little baby in the topmost house of Zuñi. Its parents were poor (bless their kind hearts!), and when they saw their cherished child recovering from a frightful eruptive malady, they were grateful; but what could they do? —phant face! When I entered, behold a very expectant, complete, and self-conscious family group! New doubts were probably troubling them as to how much I might choose to eat! The room into which I descended was the sick-room. It was also the work-room, sitting-room, dining-room, and general-purpose room of this poor family, and my little patient was—well, not healthily attractive, considering the occasion. A glance assured me that her case was not at all as I had inferred; what then could have been the meaning of this summons? I looked around inquiringly. My would-be hostess evidently interpreted it in her own way; for she nodded brightly and dived in behind the fireplace partition. All the family nodded brightly. Soon she returned with an enormous, most savory bowl of bean stew, and set it in the middle of the clean-swept, mud-floored room. Baskets, trays, bowls, and wooden platters <note>trenchers</note> were hastily arranged around this steaming center <note>nucleus</note>, with salt-pots and pepper-jars scattered among them. Then around these, in turn, were placed sitting-blocks and blankets.

“Aha!” I thought, “they are about to have their dinner, poor things. I’ll sit back here and watch them.” At which point I picked up my blanket, retired to a corner, and sat down. There was an instant look of dismay on the faces of everyone. The women looked at one another, then silently shook their heads, as if to say, “No use, not even bean stew!” At that instant, I noticed an extra stool-block. The situation dawned on me. For a second, that room spun before my eyes. Then I drew a quick, short breath, swallowed something that *would* rise in my throat, grinned (I could not smile), and nodded my head. Five adult tongues were loosened in five smiling mouths by that simple motion of my devoted head, each repeating the single victorious phrase, “*I’-tâ-na-we!*” (Let us eat).

Reader, that brief *nutation* <note>nodding of the head</note> of mine decided the fate of my relations with the Zuñi Indians. Some people have had the idea that I was “plucky” in deciding to throw myself on the generosity of a group of “barbarians” (simply, I suppose, because

Then the eating began. Everyone dipped their fingers into the hot, greasy, meaty, pepper-dyed soup with such perfect, unconcerned dexterity that I tried it myself: Goodness me! It felt as though my fingernails were scalded off. I jerked my hand out with such instant and unconscious force that my elbow struck the bristly head of a boy by my side so hard that he howled—once—then drowned his short-lived misery in more stew. I tried to cover my accident by sucking my fingers in the same manner as the others, but the stinging was so sharp that I did it too hastily for either a perfect imitation or a sense of dignified grace.

The politeness of those Indians was something so good and perfect and kind that to this day, six years later, I am grateful to them and regard them as absolute ladies and gentlemen. They neither smiled nor appeared to notice me, and by common consent made such a loud clatter and smacking of lips to cover my embarrassment that it sounded like music to my burning ears. I looked around upon

The stew was good. It tasted very much like any other bean stew.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### MORE INDIAN-MEALS

The menu of a <term>Zuñi</term> feast, even though it is made up of a single course, is sometimes as extensive and varied as that of the most luxurious civilized dinners. To be sure, no fish graces or leads into the more substantial meats in such a meal, and the soups—though numerous in variety and abundance—are hopelessly mixed up with even the desserts during the serving of it. But an examination of the illustrations considered in and brought over from our last chapter will not fail to quickly demonstrate again the vast resources of <term>Zuñi</term> cookery.

It is no wonder that within convenient reach of it, tilted up over a primitive plate of sandstone, is a skewer of broiled meat shreds; or, more often, a spindle of suet and tidbit-stuffed sheep intestines (fig. *j*), browned to brittleness at the edges but somewhat underdone toward the center. This dietary bobbin, however hot and steaming, must be—if one would have it taste its best—returned to the coals repeatedly during its course of being unwound at a long dinner. On another sandstone plate lies the blood pudding, composed of chopped liver, lungs <note>The term "lights" historically refers to the lungs of a slaughtered animal.</note>, suet, salt, pepper, coarse browned meal, brains, and clotted blood. This is rammed into a large intestine and baked or boiled until—due to its swelling and congealing when allowed to grow cold—it looks like a hugely distended Bologna sausage and tastes like unspiced head cheese. Moreover, it is certainly no less digestible. Other preparations, similar in nature to *entrées*, are exactly like this last one in outward appearance (fig. *k*). The dishes already described are only the culinary mainstays of Zuñi; for in addition to them, one may frequently see corn—sweet or common—cooked on the cob in the various ways mentioned long ago; either stewed beans or beans in large bunches (pods and all) boiled until soft and eaten as asparagus is eaten; fried, roasted, or baked squash; boiled pumpkin; snaky coils of dried melon strips—simmered with or without dried peaches, or the peaches stewed without the melon strips, both sweet without adding sugar; greens made from watercress or young milkweed pods; small game served with a rich gravy of squash-seed meal; and often the grinning, pop-eyed heads of larger game or domesticated animals, buried overnight in a stone cist <note>a stone-lined pit or box</note> topped with a fire, and as black as charcoal from the singeing they have been subjected to. The ears, hooves, and tails of deer, antelope, and cattle, first scorched in a blazing fire, then boiled

a day or two, also show up at the larger Zuñi dinners in the form of thick gelatinous soups. Finally, the most curious of all the foods of these varied meals are parched locust chrysalises, or *chum'-al-li*. These emerging, though active insects are industriously dug in great numbers from the sandy soil of the canyon woodlands by the women, who go out for their humble hunt in cheerful groups, much like berry-pickers. They are then confined in little lobe-shaped wicker cages, brought home toward evening, and immediately both cleaned and "fattened" by being soaked overnight in warmish water; if they are a lively batch, they absorb so much that they increase in size before morning to more than twice their natural bulk. Then they are taken out and given a hot bath in melted tallow, which causes them to roll up and die, after which they are salted and parched just as corn is, in an earthen toasting pot over a hot—very hot—fire.

Such a meal as this, eaten in as varied a manner as has been described, is not seen every day; but if one eliminates from

it the locusts and other fancy dishes, retaining the meat and bean stews, *he'-we*, and some other varieties of breadstuff, he will have the representative dinner, or evening meal, of every well-to-do Zuñi household almost every day (except during melon and green-corn season) throughout the year.

The breakfasts—to follow the order of importance—although simpler, are quite as substantial. They commonly consist mainly of two or three kinds of corn-dodgers, dry mush or very wet *mu'-k'ia-pa-we* (flat-dumpling soup), and meat, broiled, fried, roasted, or baked. This is the morning meal for ordinary occasions. Whatever changes take place in it on sacred feast days, when the order of things is considerably mixed up, must be mentioned later on.

During winter, breakfast is eaten at about ten o'clock. In summer, nearly half the fieldwork of the day is done before it is tasted—usually an hour later than in winter—and a luncheon intervenes between it and dinner. This lunch, taken at about two or three o'clock, is, as I have stated before, always served with *k'iäthl'-k'o-se*,

The meat must be—if prepared for the purposes it serves at luncheon—dipped in tallow or water, then broiled on a bed of coals until pliable.

A curious survival of ancient times, when the Zuñis possessed no herds and had meat only when they hunted it, is their custom of eating this jerked meat very sparingly—more to flavor the rest of the meal or to deceive the insides with the tongue, rather than as regular food. Indeed, although several strips may be lying on the little slab of sandstone beside the sauce-trough, no one except a "know-nothing Navaho" would think of taking more than one—or at the most, if the pieces are small, two of them. Immediately upon sitting down, each person chooses a strip and, dipping the end of it into the sauce, chews and sucks it until the fibers become a bit softened and separated like the bristles of a limp, irregular brush. However unpromising all this may seem, its long continuation has a proper effect. The result of this is that admirable self-control even under the difficult circumstances mentioned above. As the last phrase of this grace dies away, the food is thrown into the fire. Whether at home or abroad, I have never seen a Zuñi, young or old, taste food—even the smallest, quickest snack—without first performing this invocation or a shortened version of it. Some of the words mentioned above are among the first a child is taught to speak. Until a child can make this offering and recite this grace with his own hand and his own lips—guided and prompted by the mother—no child in Zuñi is ever officially weaned. If the child's mother dies before this happens, he is nursed by a relative who is considered his true mother from then on (according to their traditional beliefs). If it is impossible to find such a nurse, a type of porridge called *o'-k'iâs-lu*—made from sweet corn in exactly the same way *tchu'-ki-na-owe* is made from the ordinary kind—is given to the child through a cane tube fitted with a nipple made of soft cloth or membrane. I will briefly speak of the rules regulating one’s conduct at sacred feasts in our concluding chapter. Of those appropriate for ordinary occasions, yet equally applicable in either instance, I will mention a few of the more interesting ones here.

Having placed the bowls, pots, trays, and salt-jars on the floor, not far from the hearth, the women arrange stool-blocks and blankets around them, then call out “*I-tâ-na-we!*” Each person in the room must reply, “*Ya!*” or “*Te’-ä-tu’!*” (“It is well!” or “So be it!”). If they do not, the women have to repeat the summons, and not quite as mildly as they did at first. Upon sitting down, the men smack their lips, rub their hands, thrust their thumbs into their belts and give them a tug as if to loosen them, and then make the offerings. Afterward, they assume upright positions, drawing their knees up close to the body so that they occupy as little space as necessary. Before beginning to eat, a guest will, if polite, lay the

When I began to eat with the rest of the family at Zuñi, they handed first to me, as they would have first handed to any other honored guest, the one spoon they happened to possess. Reminded by this of that earlier experience, previously related, and deeply grateful thus to be saved the risk of scalding my unpracticed fingertips a second time, I nodded my thanks, took a few dips, and, oblivious to the look of expectation with which my nearest left-hand neighbor eyed the empty spoon, placed it conveniently nearby for future use. The rest did not look pleased with my lack of politeness. They evidently attributed it to ignorance, yet made a few remarks. been overlooked in haste, are not as strictly observed as they are in the presence of even a near neighbor; but such a presence, though seemingly slight, is always enough to put an entire family on their best behavior. In such a case, they would as carefully try to preserve the same unanimity at the end of a meal as at its beginning. It would be considered shameful for any of them to stop eating while anyone else remained obviously unsatisfied; and it would be equally shameful for anyone not to stop eating very soon after even one of the others—if a respected or elderly person—had done so.

When a guest or resident, man or child, stops eating, he clears his throat and exclaims, “*E’-lah-kwa! S’hâ-yu shithl-nai-e’!*” (Thanks! I have been satisfied!) The instant reply made by all the elderly women is, “*El-i’tâ!*” (Eat well!), to which the first speaker finally responds: “*Lathl-e’-lah-kwa; hâ’s-i-po-ti-k’ia!*” (Thanks again; I am full!) And the women add, “*I’tâ-i-na-we’!*” (You have eaten then!)

For instance, except when they are guests at houses other than their own, they rarely give thanks at the end of a meal; nor do they respond "Be it well" when invited to join one. As for the hostesses, they also usually sit by themselves—that is, on one side with the small children—while the men and youth sit opposite them. This strange arrangement arises from the sociological condition of the tribe, which I referred to in one of the earliest chapters of this series.

Under such a system, the husband, upon marrying, leaves his own home and goes to live with his wife as a kind of perpetual guest, not only of her clan but in her household. Within the doors of that home, he has no formal authority, except for what is granted to him by his wife. Although his hands may have tilled the fields and gathered the harvest, neither corn nor any other provisions are considered his once they have been delivered to the ladder-

At such a meal, he is thankful indeed to the old men, whom he can remember as having harassed him so much with lectures on the rules and ways of eating! He applies them all; however, all of them and more besides would not be half enough to save him, should he so far loosen the grip of his left hand on the pit of his stomach as to eat more than an amount sufficient, let us say, to satisfy a medium-sized prairie dog! No, his mother, grandmothers, aunts, older sisters, and even his maternal uncles have reminded him of the importance of eating very little, thus showing himself to be a good boarder until the match is made, or until he has proved the second point toward its ratification—his ability to hoe corn. On the distant farms, and in the far-away, lonely huts of the shepherds, these many regulations are wonderfully relaxed. At the farming towns, even the gods themselves are supposed to be more lenient (because the men are, I suppose), and the proverbial rule of comparative silence in the presence of such blessings of the beloved, such as food, is ignored. The evening meal, after the long day's work with the hoe and <term>digging-stick</term>, is merry with jokes, banter, repartee, and laughter.

But among the dark <term>piñons</term> of the mountains where the watch-houses of the herders nestle, half-underground, though no observance at meals except the invariable offering of food to the ancients be required, yet no sound other than the weird, wailing songs of the solitary occupant may be heard.

It was during the early years of my life at Zuñi that Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa, a young half-brother named Kesh'-pa-he, and I set out one sandy morning for the distant southern mesas. I say a "sandy morning," because the wind was blowing through the mountain funnels west of Zuñi in such a terrific gale that not the slightest bit of the landscape—except what was flying through the air in the form of sand—could be seen two rods ahead of us. Earth, sky, and the little river along which our trail ran were equally invisible; for far above the tops of the mesas, which were themselves a thousand feet high, the sand-clouds sail at Zuñi during the fierce winds of springtime, nor do their trailing edges ever lift themselves from the ground. Through this, shouting songs that strangely blended with the storm-voices around us, rode the two Indians, as unconcerned as ever; for their serapes, unrolled but not

And now, after the food was finished, the ashes were raked away from where our first fire had been built—"too close to the tree" (!). A few more logs were brought in and placed near the fire, and a little shelter of cedar branches was built up to keep the wind off our heads; then we stretched out to smoke our cigarettes, listen to the hunter stories of our elder brother, and make plans for tomorrow's hunting.

Island, my old brother Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa will be with me again; once more in some mimic camp which we will make, I shall listen to those ever-wondrous tales, and perhaps write them somewhere so that my readers may learn with what romances the Zuñis replace the novels of our own less active hours.<note>38</note>

That night, though the wind whistled by and cast sparks into the darkness around, we slept until fair morning and were never once awakened by cold or discomfort; for our sand-bath beds, under their covering of fragrant, springy, cedar leaves, kept warm as long as we kept our places on them, and supplied, along with the heat of our campfire, the lack of more abundant coverings.

In the morning, while Kesh'-pa-he went to find our horses, old Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa remained to prepare breakfast. He began talking of expeditions he had accompanied in which provisions had failed, and was telling me how an Indian, though almost destitute, might travel for days in the most forbidding of countries without starving.

"If he is thirsty," continued Pa'-lo-wah-ti-wa, "let him get up when the antelopes do

If he is hungry, and his arrow sees crookedly, or not at all, let him catch prairie dogs with nooses made from his own hair, or twist out a few small creatures from the roots of juniper trees and make ‘rat-brine.’ ”

Just as he was proceeding to tell me how this was done, Kesh’-pa-he appeared, leading the horses.

“There is a ‘nest’ just outside of camp!” he said.

“Where?” exclaimed Pa’-lo-wah-ti-wa, catching up his hunting knife and cutting a twig like the one with which the rabbits had been captured the evening before.

“I have been telling Little Brother how hunters make ‘rat-brine,’ ” he said with a grin, and a stirring motion of the knife he was whittling with. “He is so hungry for some that his breath is hot and his eyes are moist with anxiety! Look at him!”

Upon this, both rushed to find the “nest” in question. It was composed of sticks, stalks, and many cactus spines—with

“They’re in!” called out Kesh’-pa-he excitedly; and immediately the flexible sapling probe was inserted, twirled a few times, and withdrawn, with two squirming, wide-eyed rats well twisted to its end, and another prod brought out one more. The rats were choked *en route* to our camp, and, perhaps a little too soon for their own comfort, thrown into a bed of embers, where, after roasting a few moments, they bloated up into oblong balls, lost their tails, legs, ears, whiskers, and all other irregularities, and when pulled from the fire, looked like overdone roasted potatoes. The “rat-brine” was prepared in this way: green in color, semi-fluid, and meaty in taste (for they made me eat some of it, I am not sorry to say), and very aromatic in flavor—a quality which the rats derive from the trees in which they live and the berries and leaves on which they feed. This delicacy of the hunter would indeed be disgusting if the wood-rat of the Southwest were anything like its various Eastern representatives and relatives; but it is not. It lives on only one or two kinds of food all its life, and the peculiar flavor of the sauce made from it is due to the way in which—internal organs and all—it is worked into “rat-brine.”

I would like to tell of our personal adventures on that trip, which lasted several days longer, and of many other details of an Indian hunter’s life which I first learned about then; but I have already related, in the words of the Zuñis themselves as they adapt their own experiences into folktales, how they trail, stalk, and butcher the deer, and how they sacrifice to its <term>manes</term> <note>the spirits of the dead</note>.

# CORN FESTIVALS
->VIII<-

With the conclusion of these hunter's meals, we turn from the ordinary or secular breads of the Zuñis to their festivals of ceremony and worship, and the fasts ordained by their priests of medicine and religion.

There are two very beautiful small customs, not entirely separate from everyday life, which the Zuñis observe every year—the “presentation of bread” to the children and the “meal with the fathers.” Perhaps the most sacred, though least secret, of their esoteric societies is the *Kâ'-kâ*, or great dance organization. This is truly the church of these pagan worshippers—if they can be said to have a church—for it includes priests, laymen, and song-leaders. The public celebrations of this *Kâ'-kâ* consist of wonderfully fantastic dances, in which gods, demons, and the people of ancient times are dramatically represented by actors in costume. Inside one of the <term>estufas</term> <note>kivas</note>, or underground council chambers—which, on occasions of great importance, are decorated with fringed and feathered bows strung across their entrance ladders <note>see the initial illustration</note>—

ings. In each celebration, however, certain elements are constant. Such are the clowns—priests annually elected from the membership of the *Kâ'-kâ*, and disguised as monsters, with warty, wen-eyed, pucker-mouthed, pink masks (fig. 12), and mud-bedaubed, equally pink bodies.

First appear the dancers, some fifty of them, costumed and masked with such similarity that individuals are as indistinguishable from each other as the birds or the animals they conventionally represent. Large-jawed and staring-eyed demons of one kind or another marshal them into the open plaza of the village under the guidance of a sedate, unmasked priest bearing sacred relics and prayer-meal. One of the demons sounds a rattle and howls the first clause in the song stanza; then all fall into line, all in equal time sing the haunting song, and go through the pantomime and dance which invariably illustrate its theme. When four verses have been completed, the actors, bathed in perspiration, retire to their *estufa* <note>kiva or ceremonial chamber</note> to rest and pray, while the priest-clowns appear with drum, cabalistic <note>mystical or occult symbols</note>

They begin the most absurd, ingenious, and witty buffoonery and mockery, generally managing, nevertheless, to explain—during their apparently nonsensical dialogues—the full meanings of the dance and song. The latter is often expressed in archaic or jargon-filled terms that are utterly incomprehensible to anyone other than the initiated among the audience which throngs the terrace-tops. To merely see these clowns, without understanding a word of their incessant and really most humorous jabber, is to laugh immoderately. To understand everything, moreover, is to sometimes wish from a sheer excess of laughing that the dancers would file in and thus put an end to their jibes and antics. If these clowns accompany certain very beautiful corn dances of late autumn, then each carries a bundle of beautifully painted and feathered toy bows and arrows, or hideous dolls, with all sorts of bread loaves and cakes hanging from them. The bread tied to the bows usually takes the forms of deer, antelope, rabbits, turkeys, or other

Toward evening, when all the spectators are gathered in full force, the clowns take up their burdens of toys and go searching cautiously and grotesquely among the children as though afraid of the person they sought. When one of them finds the object of his search, he stares, wiggles, performs antics, and dodges about, approaching nearer and nearer the wondering child and extending the toy he has selected. Finally, the half-frightened little one is induced by its mother to reach for the treasure; as it clutches the offered gift, the clown suddenly straightens up and becomes grave, and delivers a long, loud-toned harangue. If the toy he has just handed is a bow and arrows, it is given to a boy; if a doll, to either a very little boy or a girl. The bow and arrows symbolize the hunt by which the little man shall, in later life,

The doll with its fanciful loaves is emblematic of housewifely skill, and, with the addition of the little human figures, of the duties and cares of motherhood. So, too, the speeches delivered with the presents correspond to the functional nature of the toys represented.

It is with these dolls, carved in imitation of the characters of the sacred dance, that the Zuñi child is first taught the simpler of the countless, tiresome prayer formulas which, as a member of the *Kâ'-kâ*, he will have to become familiar with eventually. With them, also, the young girl is first initiated into the mysteries of the life of a matron she will some day presumably lead, as well as into the simpler rituals of food consecration and hospitality.

With a few jokes that are not very delicate (for the New Year is, above all other times, the time for marriage in Zuñi), the clowns retire to their secret lodgings. There they remain until sunrise eight days later, initiating the ten newly chosen priests into the mysteries of their humor-filled vocation and severe ritual duties.

Thousands of sheep are driven in during the following days; hundreds of them and dozens of cattle are slaughtered, butchered, and piled up in the corner of the newly plastered rooms. Hunters come in from the southern wilds bringing game, and messengers speed away to surrounding tribes, bearing

I have seen in one house at such times twenty sheep carcasses, two quartered cattle, enough *he'-we* to fill a wagon-box, and numerous other dishes of the kinds already so specifically described.

On the seventh evening, the cry of the Sun-priest is heard announcing the approach of "the Gods and the Ancients." At midnight, south of the town near the foothills, watch-fires are built to guide these coming personifications—the chiefs and priests of the *Kâ'-kâ*, whose shrill flutes pipe dolefully in the night wind, and the rattles of whose masked attendants sound sharply on the frosty air. But in the midst of all these busy preparations, the “meal with the Fathers” is not forgotten. I have mentioned before that husbands leave their own homes when they marry to live in the houses of their wives. Early on the morning of New Year, however, old men may be seen tottering from place to place, gathering up their married sons and leading them to the homes of their birth. Once they have arrived there, the mother welcomes them as though they have returned from a long journey; the first bread broken on that day of all days in the Zuñi year is sacrificed in their honor on the hearth where she once saw these sons—now mostly middle-aged—frolic or play at the games they now scarcely remember.

They are ingeniously made effigies—long-haired, bearded, large-eyed, and long-snouted—so managed by means of strings and sticks by a person concealed under their ample, embroidered skirts that they seem alive and strike terror into the uninitiated.

I will not pause to tell the story of the dances and ceremonies which are performed throughout the long night by these strange masqueraders; for I have already briefly related it in the *Century* magazine for 1882. Around midnight, when fires burn most fiercely and brightly in every sacred house in Zuñi, there are stretched out across the spotless floors, like huge strings of beads, the rows and rows of round bowls, baskets, and little black cooking pots which make up the service of a great Zuñi feast.

Yet for a long time these many vessels of tempting food stand untouched; for the Sun Priest, the hereditary Priest of the House, and the Chief Priest of the Bow all in turn must recite long-winded rituals over them. Then the black-masked youth portraying the God of Fire sweeps in, carrying his burning torch of cedar bark and gracefully swinging it over each kind of food; he brushes away, as it were, the impure influences. The Priest of the Bow once more pronounces an invocation, takes a few bits of food from each dish, and hands it to

> "Thus many have the days been numbered,
> The days of our anxious awaiting,
> That we might eat with the Beloved!"

Whereupon the women echo his last clause, and the hungry crowd gathers around the bowls and baskets. Eating then becomes the main business. Except for the shouts—"Bring the salt!", "Please pass more meat this way!", "The *<term>he'-we</term>* <note>Thin, paper-like wafer bread made of cornmeal.</note> is running out down here!", "I am full, thanks!"—and the various appropriate responses, nothing is heard but the clatter of bones on the floor and the subdued smacking of lips; for ceremonial feasts are most formal, and few of the rules for showing one's appreciation at ordinary dinners are considered appropriate at these, where the gods themselves are supposed to be the hosts and hostesses.

Held once every four years, it is prepared for months beforehand, follows a fast of eight days, and lasts two days and two nights. The supplies for it are provided generously by the parents of the children for whom it is established. Indeed, extravagance in everything seems to be the order of the day.

I cannot pause to describe separately the many imaginative characters who take part in this observance. There are representations of the six-colored *Sa-la-mo-pi-a*, the Gods of the Dance, the ancient “Long-horned Demons” of war, the light-footed Tablet-dancers, and the Bird-beasts of the Mountains and Oceans. The initiates, having been strictly dieted almost to the point of starvation, are arranged in a circle around the main plaza, their backs covered with robes and blankets. To prepare them for the passage under the fringed bow of the mystical <term>estufa</term> <note>A ceremonial chamber or kiva.</note>, they are soundly beaten with long wands by each one of the forty-eight dancers, four times, with four blows given each time. When this beating is completed, they are led into the <term>estufa</term> <note>A ceremonial chamber or kiva.</note>, there to be stripped of most of their coverings and again soundly flogged, though this time fewer times. Then, indeed, their cries resound, and they wriggle to free themselves from the firm hands of their eerie captors. After this comes a grand baptism, and a breathing into the nostrils of the still-whimpering children the sacred breath of the *Kâ'-kâ*. No sooner is this done than the great effigy of the sea-serpent, moved by means of invisible cords, wriggles into their midst through a curtained porthole and vomits, with unearthly groans, a quantity of green medicine-water. By drinking this, the poor, frightened little children are freed from the probation of the <term>estufa</term>.

From housetop to housetop they go, throughout the pueblo, casting down the rarest vessels—set out to await them—and breaking up baskets and all other food vessels not hidden before their approach. As each vessel strikes the ground, the *Sa-la-mo-pi-a* rush upon it and dance it into the ground, while the baskets, as they fall, are lit by the torch of the Fire God, and soon nothing but cinders remain of their bright colors and intricate pattern-work. When it is considered that over each bowl, basket, and water-jar or cooking-pot a series of passes must be made by the tribute-collectors with their plumed wands, a prayer said, and a low, long, dirge-moan uttered, it may be understood that, naked as they are in the cold winter afternoon, theirs is no enviable task; but the end of it signals the end of the ceremonies and the beginning of the joyous feasting. ->INDIAN NOTES<-

a strange crowd of priests is gathered. The leaders of the *Kâ'-kâ* are assembled to listen to the great epic of creation, delivered by a masked and beautifully attired priest. This epic, or ritual, is the Iliad of Zuñi. It is preserved and handed down word for word by four priests; as soon as one dies, another member of the *Kâ'-kâ* is appointed to his place. One of these priests repeats every word of the ritual once in each of the six <term>estufas</term> <note>Ceremonial chambers or kivas.</note> every fourth year. Each repetition requires six hours for its delivery—thirty-six hours in total—during which time the solemn-toned, rapid-speaking priest is not allowed to taste any food other than *o'ki'äislu* water. Not once is his mask raised. No one except those in the innermost circle of the *Kâ'-kâ* is supposed to know whom they are listening to, and the community at large so reveres the office that touching the priest's garments with their fingertips, as he is carried from <term>estufa</term> to <term>estufa</term> by the ten clowns, is considered a sacred and blessed grace.

# CORN FESTIVALS
VIII

festivals I might describe are the fasts, which are no less common in Zuñi. The most important of these, because it is observed by almost everyone, is the fast following the New Year festival. When the War Gods have been placed in their shrines on Thunder Mountain and the Mount of the Beloved, and the great “Last Fire” has been lit as a signal by the Priests of the Bow, then only certain kinds of vegetable food are eaten by any man, woman, or child in Zuñi. Everyone abstains from all meat and fatty substances, and even from vessels that have been contaminated by the touch of meat. No fires are built outdoors for ten days, and many other things allowed at other times are not indulged in. The last night of the ten, however, is again full of ceremony. Once more the cooking fires are busy. At dawn, however, they are all extinguished, and the cinders and ashes are thrown to the winds of the open valley. Two nearly naked masked dancers may be seen in the twilight, swiftly making their way to a distant, lonely canyon where the God of Fire is believed to have once lived. There,

With an ancient stick and shaft, they kindle tinder by drilling the two sticks together, and lighting a torch, they hurry it back to the great central <term>estufa</term>, where matrons, young women, and young men anxiously await the gift of New Fire. As soon as the new flames are kindled from this on the hearths of the households, great baskets of food are cast into them, so that the imperishable substance of life may be wafted upward into the outer world as food for the spirits of their ancestors and those who have died during the past year. The sight of a gentle matron standing in prayer before the fireplace is by no means unbeautiful; dressed as if to meet beloved friends, she weeps softly to herself as she unsparingly casts loaf after loaf into the flames. Then, the great fast is broken by everyone except the hereditary priests, who must continue their denial of appetite for six days longer.

The purposes of the extra bowl and the turkey quill may be better implied than described when I say that I had to drink every drop—four gallons in all—of the lukewarm, nauseating drink before me. It left me weak and very empty each of those painful mornings; and after a pilgrimage to a distant shrine under the guardianship of a matron of my clan and two strong warriors, my breakfast—even though raw and stale—seemed most tempting, until I attempted to satisfy myself with it!     There is one secret order of the tribe in which initiation rules, though severe, are of quite an opposite nature. It is an esoteric society, which I mentioned in a footnote in the first chapter of this series <note>pp. 48, 632</note>, the *Ne-'-we-kwe*, or "Gluttons." Like the ten mud-priests, they are the most ridiculous clowns when they appear in public, yet the most serious of sacred personages when gathered in their secret councils. They are the medicine men *par excellence* of the tribe, whose special province is the cure of all diseases of the stomach—the elimination of poisons from the systems of the victims of sorcery or imprudence. They are exempt from all fasts, though they are denied the use of two or three kinds of delicacies for life, such as watercress and the flesh of the birds sacred to their order. His mouth is almost square, like an oven door, but with red lips—the light gleaming out when the stone door is closed—with a stiff, thin beard shooting forth from its underside. This makes it look, despite its rectangular proportions, like a cyclopean eye with heavy lashes, placed too low down. On either cheek is painted, in bright yellow, the paw of a badger or some other famous burrowing animal—this is also symbolic of his function. The creature carries in one hand a wand of yucca leaves with which to drive away dogs, and in the other a little broom of hemlock. To his backside is fastened a long cord of fiber, like the tail of a kite. As he travels along, he staggers, bends his thighs, crawls strangely from side to side, and plunges this way and that as though seeking for or trying to enter ovens; for in everything he sees nothing but ovens—he sometimes mistakes ladders or even <term>burros</term> <note>small donkeys</note> for such and tries to get into them. No sooner is he out than he turns on his captor with his yucca weapon and breaks away, plunging along to another oven, and so on, until every dome-shaped bread receptacle in the village has been duly visited and purified.

Thus, O patient reader, with thanks indeed for your long-suffering kindness in reading these hasty sketches, let us leave these ovens; let us not pollute them again with fresh bakings, or even the mention of them!

### NOTES

1. <note>See Cushing, "Outlines of Zuñi Creation Myths," *Thirteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, Washington, 1896.*</note>
2. Or the "substance of living flesh." This is illustrated, as well as possible, by the small cylinders of skin and fatty matter that can be rubbed from a person after bathing.
3. It can be seen that the Zuñis have their own way here of accounting for their primitive social organization into gentes <note>clans</note> and phratries: organizations that were nearly universal in the ancient world—as with the societies of the early Greeks and Romans—and are still prevalent among tribal groups today.
4. In ancient times, when they desired to make fire, and even today when kindling the sacred flame, the Zuñis produced and still produce the first spark by drilling with a hard stick like an arrowshaft into a dry piece of soft root. An arrowshaft is now preferred, as it is the symbol of lightning.

8. <note>This is *Tâaiyalone*, "Corn Mountain," which rises a thousand feet above the plains, about four miles southeast of Zuñi.</note>

9. The *Ne'-we-kwe*, for whom the God of Dew, or *Pai'-a-tu-ma*, was the first Great Father, are a band of medicine priests belonging—as explained previously—to one of the most ancient organizations of the Zuñis. Their medical skill is supposed to be very great in many cases, and their traditional wisdom is considered even greater. Yet they are clowns whose grotesque and quick-witted remarks amuse most public assemblies of the Pueblo holiday. One of their customs is to speak the opposite of their meaning; hence, too, their assumption of the clown's part at public ceremonies, when in reality their office and powers are to be reversed. Their grotesque costuming and face-painting are quite in keeping with their assumed characters, and would, if it were possible, justify the belief that our own circus clowns were their direct descendants or imitators. Human things are often so similar, even though geographically widely separated. See pages 620–626.

<margin>19.</margin> A priest executed about twenty years ago on the charge of witchcraft. The name is a contraction of *Po'-shai-ang-kia*, the God of Medicine Orders.

<margin>20.</margin> The kind of philosophy that can give rise to faith in this remarkable reversal of nature's order—making the growth of willows the explanation for the presence of water, instead of the consequence; making summer birds the bringers of summer instead of summer being the incentive for their yearly migration—is, strange as it may seem, the teaching of nature through her appearances, for natural philosophy is hidden beneath natural phenomena. Therefore, do not wonder at or ridicule the backward reasoning of savages. Rather, look to this—this one great difference between the child-mind and the civilized mind—as the productive cause of misunderstanding between the American and the Indian. This is a misunderstanding that will end, moreover, only with the death of this peculiar philosophy or the fate of its devoted followers.

<margin>21.</margin> Peculiarly gentle in his relations to fellow men, and never or rarely punishing his children for even the worst behavior, the Zuñi is, as a measure of self-defense, the embodiment of cruelty to crows,

<margin>23.</margin> The Apaches, Havasupai, Hualapai <note>Walapai</note>, and other Indian tribes who now inhabit the ancient territory of the Zuñis still prepare mescal, although their methods and accompanying ceremonies differ somewhat from those described above. They often purchase, however, the preparations of the tribes mentioned, reworking the material to suit their more refined tastes.

35. Literally, of the deer blood, or spirit of the deer kind or kin, born of deer. Said of a wonderfully successful or supernatural hunter.

36. In the Zuñi country, there is a kind of burrowing hornet (or carpenter bee) which drills into adobe or mud walls and there deposits its honey. On any fine day in late summer, one may see little groups of girls hunting the holes of these hornets along the garden walls. Whenever they find a number of them, they provide themselves with gourds of water which they dash against the adobe or squirt into the holes through straws. The hornets, disabled by the drenching, soon crawl out and are easily killed or driven away, after which the girls, with little wooden or bone picks, dig out the honey.

37. This point in the story depends on a play on words in the original, which can only with difficulty be translated into English. The Zuñi word for divorce is *o'k'wai*, from *o'k'o*, to crack or split, and *kwai*, to go out or be turned out. But as *o* is also a contraction of *o'we*, flour or meal, the Zuñis interpret the word in the story as “floured out” or “turned out from the flour.” There are no fewer than five versions of this story, some short and some long. I fear that the two I heard, one by Lotchi, as described in the beginning;
